1004-divine-comedy-longfellow-s-translat:
Dante Alighieri, a Florentine poet in exile, tells of a soul's passage across the realms of the dead. The road runs from the pit of Hell up the mount of Purgatory to the light of Paradise. The American poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow gave this full English version, keeping Dante's plain, steady tread.

Virgil, the Roman poet, guides Dante through Hell and Purgatory, where souls own their sins and purge them. Beatrice then leads him on to the stars. Along the way Dante meets popes, kings, friends, and foes of his own Florence. The poem stands as one of the great works of world letters, at once a story, a moral map, and a song.
1008-divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-co:
Dante Alighieri tells, in three great canticles, of a soul lost in a dark wood and led through Hell, up Purgatory's mount, and into Paradise. Henry Francis Cary's English verse, the first full version many English readers knew, carries the whole journey in blank verse of steady, grave music.

Virgil guides the poet through the damned and the penitent, while Beatrice, Dante's lost love, leads him past the spheres to God. Popes, poets, traitors, and saints crowd the road, each fixed in the fate his life earned. The poem joins story, theology, and Florentine spite into one vast design, and it still anchors the Western canon.
1061-myths-and-myth-makers-old-tales-and:
John Fiske, an American historian of the nineteenth century, argues that old myths grew from simple minds trying to explain sun, storm, and dawn. Tales of gods, heroes, and monsters, he says, began as nature poetry and hardened into faith as language and lore drifted. The book ranges from Greek gods to fairy tales and witch lore.

Fiske tests his case on dozens of stories, showing how one root tale can sprout many forms. His science is dated now, but his method, comparing tales across lands, helped found folklore study. The book remains a clear, lively guide to why humans tell such tales.
10808-consumers-cooperative-societies-in:
The Consumers' League of New York published Consumers' Cooperative Societies in New York State in April 1922, a study first prepared by Cedric Long in 1921 and revised by the League. The report sets out cooperative principles from the Rochdale Pioneers of 1844: limited interest on capital, surplus returned by patronage, and democratic control. Advice from the state's Bureau of Cooperative Associations aided the work.

The study surveys New York societies, their practice, and their prospects, for reformers and shoppers alike. Its tone is practical and hopeful about cooperation. Readers get a clear snapshot of the cooperative movement in 1920s America, with principles that still guide co-ops today.
10876-at-sunwich-port-complete:
W. W. Jacobs's At Sunwich Port, complete in twenty-five chapters with drawings by Will Owen, is a comedy of a small English seaport and its seafaring folk. The ancient port basks in July sunshine, cranes rattling in the harbor, while the town half sleeps under its tall grey church tower. Captains, sailors, shopkeepers, and young lovers fill its narrow streets.

Jem Hardy returns to find old friends and new romances, Miss Nugent among them, while Captain Nugent, Mrs. Kingdom, and Samson Wilks scheme and quarrel around him. Jacobs tells it all in his plain, funny style, with dialect and detail. Readers get the whole novel in one volume, one of his most satisfying long comedies.
11146-the-expedition-of-the-donner-party:
Eliza P. Donner Houghton wrote this history of the Donner Party, the Illinois emigrant party bound for California that was trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in 1846–47. Houghton was a child of the party, and her chapters follow the journey from the Pacific Coast in 1845, through Kansas prairie schooners, Pawnee country, and Fort Laramie.

Later chapters describe the first snow, the Reed-Snyder tragedy, Indian depredations, separation of the Donner wagons, shelter at Donner Lake and Prosser Creek, snowbound starvation, the Forlorn Hope's resort to human flesh. Houghton writes from family memory and documents, giving the fullest early account of the disaster from inside the party itself.
11160-a-cotswold-village-or-country-life:
J. Arthur Gibbs published this 1918 book, A Cotswold Village, on country life and pursuits in Gloucestershire, with illustrations. Gibbs opens flying westwards through the Thames Valley and the Old White Horse into the Cotswolds, then describes a village far from the madding crowd, an old farmhouse, the manor house.

Later chapters cover village characters, from Tom Peregrine the keeper to the village quack, the language of the Cotswolds with ancient songs and legends, life on the wolds, partridge and pigeon shooting. Gibbs worries over old grey villages, built two centuries earlier when the Cotswolds thrived, now losing population as work grows scarcer. The book preserves a Cotswold world already fading when Gibbs wrote.
11643-john-caldigate:
Anthony Trollope's John Caldigate opens at Folking and Puritan Grange, with Daniel Caldigate, the Shands, and a goldfinder among its people. Chapters carry John to Melbourne, to Nobble, and to Polyeuka Hall, then back to England.

Later chapters bring a stranger in Cambridge, a christening, Tom Crinkett at Folking, and a conclave at Puritan Grange. Hester is lured back, a wedding follows, and a trial runs through three days of evidence. The novel turns on a past marriage claim, a prison escape, and a verdict that tests family, honour, and law.
11976-dialstone-lane-complete:
Jacobs's Dialstone Lane, complete in this 1911 edition, runs to twenty-three chapters. Its illustrations hint at its comedy with captions about a creature viewed with profound contempt, a derelict punt, and a famous old Chippendale chair. Other captions show retainers instructed to make untruthful statements about their employers' whereabouts.

The full novel follows Mr. Chalk, Captain Bowers, Mr. Tredgold, and their neighbors through a treasure map, a Southern Seas expedition, and a series of marriages and misunderstandings in a seaside town. Where the separate parts break the story into portions, the complete text lets Jacobs's chain of jokes, deceptions, and reconciliations play out without interruption.
12161-night-watches-complete:
W. W. Jacobs published Night Watches in 1911, a book of ten linked comic stories set among Thames watermen and sailors ashore in London. A single night watchman narrates all of them, in dockside dialect, to an unseen listener on the wharf.

The tales run from a malingerer nursing a railway injury to a stray dog smuggled past its owner. Others follow a man made young by dye and a razor, and a handsome captain hounded by jealous wives. Each plot starts with a small fraud or vanity and ends with the schemer caught by his own plan. Together they form a compact portrait of riverside London life, told with dry humor and a sharp ear for how ordinary people talk themselves into trouble.
12215-odd-craft-complete:
W. W. Jacobs published Odd Craft in 1911, illustrated by Will Owen, gathering fourteen comic tales of sailors, villagers, and night watchmen. The book collects stories first printed in magazines, now set in one order.

Contents run from The Money-Box and The Castaway through Blundell Improvement, Bill Lapse, and Lawyer Quince. Later tales include Breaking a Spell, Establishing Relations, and The Changing Numbers, closing with Bob Pretty, Dixon Return, Avarice, The Third String, Odd Charges, and Admiral Peters. Each tale starts with a small scheme or vanity and ends with the schemer caught. Together they form Jacobs most sustained comic world: Thames wharves, country pubs, and men who talk themselves into trouble.
12242-poems-by-emily-dickinson-three-ser:
Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson edited this complete edition of Emily Dickinson poems, gathering three series into one volume. Dickinson, who died in 1886, wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems, most unpublished in her lifetime and kept in portfolios.

The preface, quoting Emerson phrase poetry of the portfolio, explains that Dickinson wrote without thought of publication, solely to express her own mind. Poems on death, nature, love, and faith follow in short, dash-broken lines, with slant rhymes and sudden turns. The editors regularized some punctuation, a choice later scholars debated. Even so, the volume introduced most readers to a poet whose private verse remade American poetry from a room in Amherst.
12426-routledge-s-manual-of-etiquette:
George Routledge and Sons published Routledge Manual of Etiquette, covering etiquette for ladies and gentlemen, a ball-room companion, courtship and matrimony, how to dress well, how to carve, and toasts and sentiments. The manual served Victorian readers who wanted rules for new social situations.

Contents for ladies run from introductions and morning calls through conversation, dress, dinner tables, and ball rooms. A mid-book dance figure has the lady at the bottom advance, give right hands, and swing quickly round, while partners mirror the move. The book also covers staying at a friend house, breakfast, and luncheon. It is a practical guide to manners, now a social history of how Victorians danced, dined, and courted.
12770-a-study-of-the-topography-and-muni:
Ralph Van Deman Magoffin's 1908 Johns Hopkins study takes on Praeneste, the ancient Latin town now called Palestrina, near Rome. The first part maps its walls and gates, water supply, forum, sacred road, and great temple of Fortuna Primigenia. Stones and inscriptions, not guesswork, fix where each feature stood.

The second part asks how the town was run, first as a municipium and later as a Roman colony, and lists its officers in order. Magoffin weighs the evidence for each office and rank with care. The study suits readers of Roman history who want a town seen whole, stone by stone and office by office.
12830-the-perfect-tribute:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews wrote this short 1908 tale about Abraham Lincoln's trip to Gettysburg in November 1863. A special train from Washington carries judges, cabinet men, and the army chief to consecrate the national cemetery, with Lincoln sad, awkward, and ill-dressed among them. The quiet landscape slips past as he broods.

At Gettysburg his brief address meets silence, not applause, and Lincoln fears he has failed his best effort. Only Edward Everett's warm words after the ceremony hint at what the speech will become. The story is a tender, famous imagining of the Address finding its audience slowly.
12879-voices-for-the-speechless-selectio:
Abraham Firth compiled Voices for the Speechless in 1883 for schools and private reading, as secretary of the American Humane Association. Longfellow and Cowper supply the mottoes: verse that stands between an animal and woe. Moral lessons open the book, praising the ox for patient toil and the horse and dog for loyal zeal.

An Arab horse tale shows the theme: a captive master, bound hand and foot, is seized by the girdle and carried home at full speed through the night. Bird poems plead against killing songbirds for a handful of grain. The book is an earnest Victorian plea for kindness to animals.
13042-knickerbocker-s-history-of-new-yor:
Washington Irving's Knickerbocker's History of New York, published in December 1809 when Irving was twenty-six, first won him wide fame. The book pretends to be a solemn history of New York by Diedrich Knickerbocker, but it is in fact a long comic satire on Dutch settlers, governors, and politics. Walter Scott wrote that he had never read anything so jocose.

Irving fills his mock history with specters, hobgoblins, and a commodore who swears he saw porpoises broiled on a gridiron. He also mocks war itself, praising gunpowder as the grand mark of reason, while brutes make do with horns. The satire is broad and learned at once, and it made Irving's name on both sides of the Atlantic.
13073-mr-trunnell-mate-of-the-ship-pirat:
T. Jenkins Hains's 1900 sea novel follows a mate who finds himself on the beach at Melbourne, out of a berth and short of cash. The narrator, twenty-five and seven years at sea, had never tasted rum, and he refuses to ship before the mast on the first vessel out. A threatening landlord soon forces his hand, and he joins the ship Pirate.

At sea, a great wave breaks five feet above the bulwarks and sweeps the main deck, smashing rails, boats, and rigging. Later, the crew works a leak from a frame slung outboard, studying the bilge through calm water. Hains writes from sailor's knowledge, and his tale mixes storm, wreck, and shipboard scheming with a plain seaman's voice.
1312-selected-stories-of-bret-harte:
Bret Harte's chosen tales of the California gold rush gather here: gamblers, miners, and dance-hall girls in camps where luck turns on a card and sentiment hides under rough speech. "The Luck of Roaring Camp" and "The Outcasts of Poker Flat" lead the selection.

Harte writes the West with irony and tenderness, and his stories made California famous in the East. The tales are short, polished, and often surprising. The book gives the best of Harte in one volume, and it still reads as the classic gold-rush fiction.
13356-the-captain-s-toll-gate:
Frank R. Stockton's 1903 Captain's Toll-Gate, with a memorial sketch by Mrs. Stockton, follows Olive, Maria Port, Mrs. Easterfield, and Captain Asher at a country toll-gate. Chapters run from Olive paying toll and Mr. Claude Locker to a fishing trip, a drive with the butcher, a bicycle trip, and the captain and Dick Lancaster deserting the toll-gate. Stockton writes gentle comedy of manners.

Dick Lancaster walks six miles to Broadstone on a fine morning while the captain goes to Glenford on business, thinking of Olive all the way and missing her grievously. Later, talk never flags, yet no one cares for it, since all think of the conflict of serenades and what might happen next. The novel is a charming, old-fashioned romance.
1346-the-eighteenth-brumaire-of-louis-bo:
Karl Marx wrote this short history in the wake of Louis Bonaparte's coup of December 1851, which ended the French Second Republic. Looking back over 1848 to 1851, he traces how a republic born in revolt passed through party strife, street fighting, and parliamentary deadlock until one man seized power.

Marx reads the coup not as a freak but as the outcome of class fears, peasant votes, and a state machine grown strong enough to stand above society. His famous line on history repeating as farce frames the whole account. The book remains a classic study of how democracies can undo themselves.
13464-essays-on-taste:
The Augustan Reprint Society pairs John Gilbert Cooper's Letters Concerning Taste, third edition 1757, with John Armstrong's Miscellanies of 1770, introduced by Ralph Cohen. Together they ask what taste is, how it is learned, and why some people seem born without a spark of it.

Cooper and Armstrong argue in verse and prose, mocking talk learned by rote at coffee houses and schools, and praising a polished soul that receives images without warping them. Virgil, admired by Maecenas and hated by a later monster, stands as a test of natural writing. The volume gives modern readers two eighteenth-century voices on judgment, style, and honest art.
1364-tom-swift-and-his-electric-locomoti:
Tom Swift takes on the rails in this boy inventor tale, when a tempting offer asks him to build an electric locomotive faster than any train alive. Rivals, saboteurs, and a signed contract raise the stakes, and Tom must prove his engine on the track while enemies work in the dark.

With Ned Newton and Koku beside him, Tom tests speed, power, and safety, and the trial run becomes a race against time and treachery. The book is full of workshop talk, narrow escapes, and boyish confidence. It is a lively piece of early electric-age adventure for young readers.
13931-master-of-his-fate:
J. Maclaren Cobban published Master of His Fate in 1890, a novel of medicine, mystery, and hypnotism. Julius Courtney, a mysterious case, and M. Dolaro open the contents. The remarkable case of Lady Mary Fane, strange scenes in Curzon Street, and an apparition with a confession follow. A love interlude softens the mystery.

Cobban dedicates the book to a doctor friend, praising humane and exacting healers. The good doctor of the story, born surgeon and ever young, stands for self-forgetful care. A scene under an umbrella, where a woman feels strength leave her, hints at mesmeric power. The novel mixes sensation with medical interest. It suits fans of Victorian mystery fiction.
14300-the-life-of-napoleon-i-complete:
John Holland Rose's full life of Napoleon draws on British official records and on French sources. It follows the Corsican officer from his rise through empire, exile, and the Hundred Days. Rose sets battles beside treaties, and ambition beside the limits of power. The book first appeared in 1901 and grew through new editions to 1910. It stands as a solid, readable life for general readers and students alike.

Rose shows Napoleon pressing Britain over émigré journals in London, and Britain refusing to curb its press at his dictation. His Moniteur answered London's pop-guns with double-shotted retorts, yet no formal complaint came. In Spain, a sickly general thrust into command could not hold Wellington at bay, and the recall of abler men sealed the failure. Wellington ranked Soult second only to Masséna among French marshals. The book judges Napoleon by his acts, not by legend.
14314-etiquette:
Emily Post wrote Etiquette in 1922, a guide to manners in society, business, politics, and at home. It covers dinners, calls, weddings, and letters, with photographs and copies of social forms. Post writes for a new age of American wealth, where good taste must be learned, not born. The book mixes firm rules with stories of real folk. Its voice is warm, sure, and often amused.

At dinner the butler counts heads, warns the cook, and tells the hostess the meal is served. The host leads the lady of honor in, and guests follow two by two, hostess last. Place cards settle seats at formal meals. A second scene shows a bride's visit to a white shingled house, where a maid in silver grey taffeta opens the door. Post's rules aim at ease: manners should hide effort and spare others trouble.
14712-vandover-and-the-brute:
Frank Norris's Vandover and the Brute, published in 1914 after the author's death, follows a young San Franciscan whose memory keeps only scattered scenes of his life. One early memory is the family's move from Boston to San Francisco when Vandover was about eight.

As a man, Vandover bathes and sails on the bay and rides out with greyhounds to course jack-rabbits. He plans a European trip with his father, yet feels himself changed, older, and more serious. The title's brute is the coarse force within him that his good manners cannot tame. Norris writes a naturalist novel of appetite, habit, and slow ruin.
14715-the-house-in-good-taste:
Elsie de Wolfe's The House in Good Taste, published by the Century Company in 1913 and illustrated with photographs, is a pioneer guide to interior decoration by America's first professional decorator. De Wolfe argues for houses shaped by their owners' lives.

Chapters cover suitability, simplicity, and proportion, then walls, color, doors, windows, and chintz. Artificial light, halls, and each room from drawing-room to dressing-room and bath follow. She urges planning electric light early, with base openings laid out while the house is still in embryo. The book remains a readable classic of tasteful, livable rooms.
14853-the-stowmarket-mystery-or-a-legacy:
Louis Tracy's 1904 mystery, subtitled a legacy of hate, opens with the Stowmarket mystery itself. David Hume's story, a dream, a view through the library window and a figure from behind the hedge follow. An old acquaintance, husband and wife and revelations follow.

A ko-katana, a black museum, Mr. Okasaki, what the stationmaster saw and two women deepen the puzzle, before Margaret speaks out, an unexpected visitor arrives and cousins are sought with the cry to seek the woman. Tracy, author of Wings of the Morning, writes a busy Edwardian detective tale where an old hate poisons the present and every clue points two ways.
15240-a-journal-of-a-tour-in-the-congo-f:
Marcus Dorman's journal of a tour in the Congo Free State, first published in 1905 and dedicated to King Leopold II, reproduces his diary with minimal editing. He wanted impressions gained on the spot to stand without later polish. The tour runs through a colony then under fierce scrutiny abroad.

Dorman writes as a British observer of empire, noting administration, trade, and travel with a period eye. His dedication to Leopold marks the book's stance, and modern readers should weigh it against later knowledge of Congo abuses. As a travel record, it offers a detailed, if partial, view of the Free State.
15490-the-young-lady-s-mentor-a-guide-to:
An anonymous lady published this guide to the formation of character in Philadelphia in 1852, in a series of letters to her unknown friends. The first letter, on contentment, says only the young can be hopefully addressed, since habits of mind soon form and harden. That urgency runs through the whole book.

Later letters take up temper, falsehood and truthfulness, envy, selfishness, self-control, economy, and the cultivation of the mind. Amusements, the influence of women on society, the education of women, love and marriage, and literary gifts for women follow. The mentor's counsel is earnest and practical: guard the temper, tell the truth, spend wisely, and use influence for good. It is a clear record of mid-century ideals for young women.
15718-how-to-write-special-feature-artic:
A handbook for magazine writers by Willard Grosvenor Bleyer, director of journalism at the University of Wisconsin. Houghton Mifflin issued it in 1919, after Bleyer's earlier books on news writing. The book teaches reporters, correspondents, and free-lance writers to sell special articles. Its field is the popular magazine and the newspaper magazine section.

Bleyer maps the field, then shows how to find subjects, gather facts, and shape a piece for a given market. Human interest, explanation, and how-to articles each get practical rules. Examples stress clear leads, honest detail, and a strong close. The handbook still helps new writers: it treats feature writing as a craft with markets, deadlines, and readers, not as mere inspiration.
15940-the-luck-of-the-mounted-a-tale-of-:
A Mounted Police tale by Sergeant Ralph S. Kendall, ex-member of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1920. Kendall dedicates the book to his old comrades, present and ex-members, with every kind thought. An Ingoldsby epigraph promises that murder will out, though the blood-spiller double and fly. The first chapter sings of days gone by.

Mounted men ride the north-west trails, tracking crime through snow, bush, and settlement. Witchcraft and sorcery, the epigraph warns, cannot save a killer from hue and cry. Kendall writes from service, with a policeman's eye for detail. The tale delights as a northern adventure: law on horseback, and luck that favours the steadfast.
15968-the-grounds-of-christianity-examin:
A rationalist examination of Christianity by George Bethune English, issued in Boston in 1813. English takes Isaiah for his motto: first understand, then judge, and bring forth witnesses. He dedicates the book to the intelligent and candid, willing to listen to every opinion supported by reason. His method compares the New Testament with the Old.

Chapter one shows how apostles and authors of the New Testament endeavour to prove Jesus from prophecy. English tests each claim against the Hebrew text, with reason as judge. His tone stays calm and learned, not mocking. The book stands as an early American freethought classic: faith, examined by its own book, in open court.
1604-the-ebb-tide-a-trio-and-quartette:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Lloyd Osbourne's Ebb-Tide opens on a beach at night in the Pacific, where scattered men of many European races carry activity and spread disease, some prospering, some vegetating. Three beachcombers, Herrick, Davis, and Huish, seize a stolen ship and sail toward a pearl island and ruin.

The trio's voyage becomes a study of failure, faith, and the South Seas, with a fanatic planter as their final judge. Stevenson's prose is lean and dark. The Ebb-Tide is a powerful late work, a tale of empire's outcasts that ends in a strange, stern redemption.
16131-campaign-pictures-of-the-war-in-so:
A. G. Hales, special correspondent of the Daily News, published these letters from the front with Cassell in 1901. Dedicated to Sir John Robinson, the Daily News manager who gave Hales his chance after twenty years of waiting, the book follows the war in South Africa through Australian eyes. Chapters cover Australia on the march, a prisoner of war, stopping a few, Australia at the war, and Slingersfontein.

Hales writes as a reporter among soldiers, with battle, camp, and column life in vivid, first-hand detail. His Australian angle gives the Boer War a fresh voice, proud and rough-edged. Readers of war reporting and imperial history will find a lively, on-the-ground account.
16146-petty-troubles-of-married-life-com:
Honore de Balzac's Petty Troubles of Married Life opens with the unkindest cut of all, a trouble profound for sons-in-law and daughters-in-law yet petty for parents. A ten-times-happy husband at the baptism of his eleventh child, the little last newcomer, exclaims that a child costs terribly dear. Balzac then names his type-wife Caroline, charming like all young ladies, married four months to a lawyer, captain, engineer, judge, or young viscount.

Each short section turns a small domestic sting into comedy and moral anatomy, from money to in-laws to vanity. Balzac writes with a keen, amused eye for married life's daily friction. Readers of French realism will enjoy these sharp, funny sketches of the household battlefield.
16151-the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-6:
Volume one, number six of The Continental Monthly, dated June 1862, shows a Civil War magazine of literature and national policy at work. Its pages carry an editorial quarrel over articles in the Boston Courier said to reprint, word for word, a Knickerbocker Magazine series from 1847. The editors insist they spoke guardedly, lacking more than a few Courier numbers, yet hold that several columns were literal reprints.

An advertisement for Hazard's railroad and military map of the Southern states, compiled from Coast Surveys and a personal tour, sits nearby, a reminder that readers wanted war geography. The number captures wartime print culture: argument, accusation, and practical news side by side. Historians of the press will find it a lively artifact.
16220-rambles-in-the-mammoth-cave-during:
Alexander Clark Bullitt's 1845 Louisville book records a visitor's rambles in Mammoth Cave during 1844. The publisher's advertisement answers frequent calls from intelligent visitors to the city for some account of the great cave, and Bullitt supplies it in a chatty, wondering style. Underground passages, vast rooms, and strange formations fill his pages, with the cave's pure air and even temperature noted throughout.

An errata page corrects a passage on invalids in the cave, a reminder that the age hoped cave air might cure lung disease. The book captures early American cave tourism at its most earnest and curious. Modern readers can follow a nineteenth-century explorer into Kentucky's underworld with a lively guide.
16434-autobiography-of-friedrich-froebel:
Emilie Michaelis and H. Keatley Moore translated and annotated this autobiography of Friedrich Froebel, founder of the kindergarten, issued at Syracuse in 1889. A long letter to the Duke of Meiningen forms the core. It traces Froebel from birth and early life through apprenticeship to a forester, Jena University, clerkships, and teaching at the Frankfurt Model School.

Visits to Pestalozzi, private tutoring, and the road to Yverdon fill the later pages. The motto, Come, let us live for our children, sums up Froebel's creed. For students of education, the book gives the kindergarten idea straight from its maker's own life story.
16534-a-young-folks-history-of-the-churc:
Nephi Anderson wrote this young folks' history of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints for the Deseret Sunday School Union, copyrighted 1889 and reprinted in 1916. Chapters move from a parable and the First Vision through the angel Moroni, the sacred plates, and the Book of Mormon. The restoration of the priesthood, persecution, Ohio, and Zion's Camp follow.

Anderson addresses parents and teachers directly, hoping church history will plant loyalty and love for its heroes in boys and girls. The tone is simple and devout. The book serves as a clear statement of how the church taught its own story to its young in the early twentieth century.
16752-caste:
W. A. Fraser wrote this 1922 novel of India under British rule, issued by George H. Doran in New York. It opens at Poona, where three Mahratta chiefs plot the overthrow of the British, and priests at the Parvati temple pray for the ruin of the hated whites. Each priest lays marigolds at the idol's feet, while Dandhu Panth, adopted son of the Peshwa, moves in the marble palaces below.

Fraser sets caste, faith, and revolt against empire in a tale of plots and palaces. The novel reflects its age's views of India, which modern readers will read with care. As a period adventure, it offers color, intrigue, and a fast plot of conspiracy in the years before the Mutiny's shadow fell.
1704-pierrette:
An orphan girl named Pierrette is sent to live with cousins in the town of Provins. The cousins take her in for show and then starve her of food, kindness, and schooling. Her cousins, the Rogrons, welcome her only for show, then deny her food, kindness, and schooling, while the town watches and does little.

Balzac builds the case against the Rogrons piece by piece: small cruelties, withheld letters, and a household run on spite. The novella's anger is quiet but steady. It ends as a warning about what happens when a child has no one willing to stand between her and people who profit from her helplessness.
17216-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume one complete, gathers the famous comic weekly from its first Saturday issues. Its introduction promises a refuge for destitute wit, orphan jokes, and perishing puns, plus freedom for jokes of all nations. Departments cover politics without party prejudice, fashions by Mrs. J. Punch, police reports by a noble regular, and reviews of books and plays.

The volume sets the tone for a century of British satire: sharp, funny, and fond of small change and big targets alike. Readers who love Victorian humor will find cartoons, jokes, and squibs at their freshest. It is a landmark first volume, still lively for anyone curious about how Punch learned to laugh at power.
17579-the-history-of-napoleon-buonaparte:
John Gibson Lockhart, who lived from 1794 to 1854, wrote this history of Napoleon Buonaparte, issued here in a Dent edition first published in February 1906 and reprinted through March 1915. Lockhart presents Napoleon as a figure of fiery energy and irresistible ambition, whose career later ages would look back on as a grand and supernatural romance. That romantic view colours the whole narrative.

Readers follow Napoleon from youthful fire through magnificent progress to fall, in the vivid style of a nineteenth-century man of letters. The book serves as an introduction to Napoleon for general readers, and as a period piece in how Britain once told his story. Its pace and colour keep a long life moving swiftly.
17867-the-helpmate:
May Sinclair wrote The Helpmate in 1907, issued in New York by Henry Holt. Sinclair, author of The Divine Fire and Audrey Craven, was a keen observer of marriage, faith, and the inner life, and this novel is one of her most searching studies.

The tale follows a wife bound to a husband whose failings test her patience, pride, and faith to the edge. Sinclair writes with a sharp, modern eye for motive, and she lets her heroine think, doubt, and choose. The book still grips as a portrait of a marriage under strain, and as an early modern novel of a woman's mind.
18035-marjorie-at-seacote:
Carolyn Wells wrote Marjorie at Seacote in 1912, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, by arrangement with Dodd, Mead. Wells, author of the Patty books, here sends Marjorie to the shore for a summer of fun.

Chapters run from Kitty's dinner and Tom, Dick, and Harry to the sand club, sand court, the jolly sandboy, and the glorious Fourth. A king bows so low his cape falls off, and a search and a revelation spice the term. Wells writes bright, clean girls' fiction. It is a sunny seaside tale, full of play, chums, and summer joy.
18087-historic-doubts-relative-to-napole:
Richard Whately wrote Historic Doubts Relative to Napoleon Buonaparte, first printed in 1819 and reissued in London in 1865. Whately, an archbishop and logician, uses Hume's essay on miracles to ask how we know what we claim to know.

He argues, in jest and in earnest, that the same strict tests that skeptics use on miracles would, if pressed, cast doubt on Napoleon's very existence. Readers took the pamphlet both as a joke and as a serious tract, and Whately notes the mix-up with amusement. It is a witty, classic piece on evidence, belief, and the rules of fair doubt.
18320-marine-protozoa-from-woods-hole-bu:
Gary N. Calkins of Columbia University wrote this 1901 paper for the Bulletin of the United States Fish Commission. Calkins worked at Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and noted that little had been done in America on marine protozoa, the tiny one-celled creatures of the sea. Earlier notes by Kellicott, Stokes, and Peck were brief, and only one paper treated a single form at length.

Calkins watched water and algae fresh from the sea for two months, from July 1 to September 1, without a tow-net or dredge. He records the forms he found, their shapes, and their place as food for larger sea life. Readers get a careful field record from the early days of marine biology, when a summer at a shore station could still map a whole neglected group.
18575-one-hundred-merrie-and-delightsome:
Robert B. Douglas first put these hundred French tales into English in this 1899 Paris edition, from the collection known as Les Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles, edited by Antoine de la Salle. The tales are short, witty, and frank about love, marriage, and trickery, meant to be told in good company for joy and laughter. Each story ends with a neat twist or jest.

The set ranges from an abbess cured by her nuns' pact to a lawyer's wife caught by a line. It adds a count foiled by his leggings and a husband shut in a clothes chest. Clerks, counts, damsels, and knights crowd the pages. Readers get a merry, adult-flavored glimpse of late medieval French storytelling.
18952-boy-scouts-on-a-long-hike-or-to-th:
Archibald Lee Fletcher published this Boy Scout story in Chicago in 1913. Its heroes are the boys of the Beaver Patrol, who set out on a long hike that carries them into camp life in Alabama and then into the Black Water Swamps. Chapter titles promise a runaway balloon, a trail through country where no foot has trod, and an oasis found in the swamp.

The heart of the tale is a rescue: the patrol must reach people in danger and bring help in time, testing their skill, courage, and teamwork. Fletcher stresses duty, kindness, and resourcefulness over mere adventure. Readers get a period scout story that shows the movement's early ideals in action, told for boys of its own day.
19752-quisante:
Quisanté is an English novel of a commanding, difficult hero. Raphael Quisanté's family anchors the story's past. His sister raised the younger Quisanté from childhood. She served him and believed in him, yet never liked him. She never offered him her love either. That cold loyalty shapes the book's emotional weather.

The novel belongs to Anthony Hope's shelf of polished society fiction. Hope, famous for The Prisoner of Zenda, also wrote drawing-room studies like this. Power, duty, and dislike mix in its households. Readers watch belief without affection do its slow work. The book is a quieter Hope, built on character. It rewards readers who like tension under good manners.
2013-the-pit-prop-syndicate:
Freeman Wills Crofts sets a detective novel among timber traders in France and England, where pit props, the wooden supports used in mines, become the cover for a shady business scheme. Seymour Merriman, an ordinary man on a motor tour, drifts into the deal and soon finds himself out of his depth. Crofts, an engineer by training, builds his plots on timetables, maps, and careful detail.

The first half follows the amateurs as cargoes move, depots change hands, and pressure builds. A murder then brings in Inspector Willis, who traces clues, listens in, and slowly exposes the syndicate behind the shipments. Methodical detection, not action, drives the second half to its close. The slow unravelling, with false leads and patient police work, became a hallmark of Crofts's detective fiction.
20154-invaders-from-the-infinite:
John W. Campbell published Invaders from the Infinite in 1961, a space opera of vast powers. Chief Pilot Russ Evans hears frantic calls to lower a wavelength. A voice mocks a foe who thinks he is a sun. In truth, that foe is just a planetoid, the voice sneers.

Campbell edited famed science fiction magazines and shaped the field for decades. His tales pit human wits against cosmic forces and alien minds. Ships hide in far, lonely spots three-quarters of a billion miles out. Readers get big-scale space war in the classic pulp style Campbell loved.
20216-old-time-makers-of-medicine-the-st:
Old-Time Makers of Medicine tells of the students and teachers of the Middle Ages. A French history of surgery from 1774 opens the book's case. In reading this history, one finds modern finds that are not new. Many cures seem to have been made twice, centuries apart.

Medieval doctors worked with prayer, herbs, astrology, and bold surgery alike. The book traces schools, texts, and famed healers of that long age. It honors forgotten men who kept medical learning alive through dark times. Readers get a warm, learned tour of medicine before the modern era.
2027-tartuffe-or-the-hypocrite:
Moliere's famous comedy, in Curtis Hidden Page's translation, exposes a pious fraud who worms his way into a rich household. Orgon, the head of the house, trusts Tartuffe so fully that he gives him money, lodging, and even his daughter's hand. Moliere first staged Tartuffe in 1664, and church and court fought over it, which only raised its fame.

Family members see through the act and plot to unmask him, but Orgon will not listen until the trap closes on himself. The play mixes sharp satire on false religion with fast comic scenes, and it still bites in any age of smooth-talking rogues. Page's translation keeps the verse clear for English readers, so the jokes land without a knowledge of French.
20295-my-new-curate:
My New Curate is a novel of an Irish parish priest and his young helper. The old priest admits he was too free with his tongue once. In bitterness he asked what a bishop can do with a parish priest. A parish priest is independent of him, he said, unwisely and rudely.

Those words, bad grammar and all, were carried to the bishop. His lordship's dry reply opens a tale of clash and growth. Irish parish novels mix humor, faith, and village character richly. Readers get a warm, witty story of two priests learning to work together.
20317-a-treatise-on-staff-making-and-piv:
A Treatise on Staff Making and Pivoting teaches watchmakers a fine, exact craft. Some lathe workers give no thought to the form of pivots, it warns. Others make pivots faultless in shape but bungling in finish. Either fault can spoil the good work of the other half.

Watch staffs and pivots are tiny parts on which timekeeping turns. The treatise gives full directions, tools, and methods for making them well. Such manuals kept rare hand skills alive in the machine age. Readers get precise craft knowledge from the bench of a master watchmaker.
20320-jack-harkaway-s-boy-tinker-among-t:
Bracebridge Hemyng wrote Jack Harkaway's Boy Tinker Among the Turks, book fifteen in a series. A stern voice warns a young gentleman in the stirrups to remember command. His thirst for excitement, he is told, may compromise everyone aboard. He is urged to reflect before he adds anything worse to the row.

Jack Harkaway was a hero of cheap, thrilling tales for boys. Among the Turks promises disguise, capture, escape, and bold rescue abroad. Tinker, his loyal companion, shares each scrape and triumph with him. Readers get penny-dreadful adventure at full gallop, in the classic mold.
20470-etiquette:
Etiquette, published in 1892, is a guide to correct behavior in social life. It defines its subject at the start. Etiquette, it says, covers the manner of actions and the showing of a proper social spirit through set forms and ceremonies.

Polite usage, the book goes on, recognizes certain rules for calls, dinners, dress, and introductions. To break them marked a person as careless or ill-bred. Such manuals mattered greatly in the nineteenth century. A growing middle class wanted the rules of the drawing room written down plainly, to learn at home.
20528-round-about-a-great-estate:
Richard Jefferies wrote Round About a Great Estate about the country world around a large landed property. Jefferies was the finest English nature writer of his age. Here he watches the farmers, laborers, and gamekeepers of one estate through the seasons.

He notes a hopeful change among the workers. The laborer is now well grounded in basic education, and reads and writes with ease. He is not without knowledge of the higher sort either. Jefferies sets such social change inside loving descriptions of fields, woods, and weather, in prose that made him famous.
20615-the-master-knot-of-human-fate:
Ellis Meredith's The Master-Knot of Human Fate, published in 1901, is a novel of the Rocky Mountain West. From the heights, a town lies plain below in the clear air. It looks, the narrator says, like a bird's-eye map rather than an actual town.

Far away to the left stand strangely piled rocks, gorgeous in coloring and grotesque in outline. In that high, bright country, Meredith sets a story of love, mining fortunes, and hard moral choice. The master-knot of the title is the tie no character can undo without loss.
20798-the-strand-magazine-vol-05-issue-2:
At Sandringham, the Prince drops state cares and turns country gentleman, says The Strand Magazine for April 1893. He farms, minds his tenants, and joins his wife in school and sick visits. Sketches, dairy work, and needlework fill the family's quiet days.

Volume five, issue twenty-eight holds tales, interviews, and art in the Strand's famed mix. The magazine made Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes a household name in these years. Its illustrated pages set the tone for middle-class reading of the age. One issue like this freezes the tastes and heroes of 1893 in print.
20901-in-apple-blossom-time-a-fairy-tale:
Miss Upton, worn from hours of hard shopping, sinks into a cafe seat with relief. Clara Louise Burnham opens In Apple-Blossom Time, from 1919, on that flushed, tired figure. Her scarlet face shows how keen she was to claim the last free table.

Burnham calls her tale a fairy tale brought up to date. Plain folk, kind hearts, and a touch of magic shape its course. Apple blossom season sets its bloom over love and fresh starts. Burnham's wholesome tales sold widely in her day, and this one keeps her blend of humour, warmth, and firm faith in goodness.
21580-the-pirate:
A dismasted hull wallows in the Bay of Biscay at the start of Captain Marryat's The Pirate, published in 1836. The wreck is a remnant of a fourth ship, waterlogged and awash in heavy seas. It is late June in the year seventeen hundred and ninety something.

Sun breaks through as the gale dies, pouring light over the troubled water. From wreck and rescue the tale moves into piracy on the high seas. The Pirate was Marryat's ninth book, written with his usual speed of invention. Few writers could open a sea tale with such force of wind and wave.
21693-post-haste:
R. M. Ballantyne builds Post Haste on the facts of the British post, drawn from official reports. He thanks the Postmaster-General's staff and Sir Arthur Blackwood for their help. Visits to the General Post Office in London furnished much of the tale.

A bay of mighty cliffs, smugglers, and Atlantic billows frames the human story. A widow named Maylands takes a lonely cottage on that wild coast to open the plot. Letters lost, delayed, and delivered drive chapter after chapter. Ballantyne aims to show postal work across the kingdom, and to amuse while he informs.
21813-the-madman-and-the-pirate:
A pirate-looking schooner rests in a still Pacific lagoon at the opening of this Ballantyne tale. A shark's fin cuts the glassy water, and an albatross studies the deck from above. Yet the schooner is said to be an honest trader, though her trade is a mystery. Her crew mixes sedate Englishmen with Lascars and Malays of rougher looks.

Ballantyne sets his scene on a coral island like a gem on the ocean's breast. The madman and the pirate of the title wait in the wings of that calm. Storm, treachery, and strange company follow in his classic island manner. Readers of The Coral Island will feel at home: beauty first, then danger close behind it.
21881-the-life-of-the-waiting-soul-in-th:
What happens between death and the last day is R. E. Sanderson's subject in these addresses, first given in Chichester Cathedral in 1896. Sanderson, canon of Chichester and former headmaster of Lancing College, says the topic had dropped out of English Christian thought. His plain words to an ordinary congregation aim to wake fresh interest in it. The book ran to five editions by 1900.

He explains what he believes can be known about the intermediate life, the waiting of the soul. He promises nothing new, holding that newness here would likely mean error. Doctrines like universalism he leaves aside as belonging to another period. The tone is pastoral, not combative: comfort for the curious and the bereaved.
21917-eingeschneit-eine-studentengeschic:
German students get snowed in, as the title promises, in Emil Frommel's Eingeschneit, a student story edited for American learners by Wilhelm Bernhardt. This Heath school edition of 1908, first copyrighted in 1899, prints the story in German with an introduction, notes, and vocabulary. Fraktur type in the original is marked in this text with braces. Numbered notes guide the student through hard words page by page.

The tale opens on the road: two young men leave their uncle and aunts behind and ride gladly toward the railway station. A wedding carriage, garlanded, crosses their world in the early pages. Frommel was a beloved German storyteller and court preacher. As a reader, the book teaches German by charm: a warm tale first, a lesson second.
2193-a-ward-of-the-golden-gate:
A young woman placed under guardianship in San Francisco learns to navigate money, marriage, and her own will. Bret Harte sets this novel in the Golden Gate city of the gold rush aftermath, where new wealth and old manners meet uneasily. The ward at its center must sort true friends from fortune hunters.

Harte gives the story his usual blend of wit and local color, with drawing rooms, mines, and city streets all in play. The heroine's growth from a sheltered girl to a woman who can judge character is the real plot. It is a pleasant, well-made romance of California society finding its feet.
21959-letters-from-a-self-made-merchant-:
A Chicago pork-packer writes his boy at Harvard in George Horace Lorimer's Letters from a Self-Made Merchant to His Son, published in 1902. John Graham, known on the exchange as Old Gorgon Graham, heads Graham and Company at the Union Stock Yards. His son Pierrepont, called Piggy by his friends, has just joined the freshman class. The father's letters mix business gospel with jokes at his son's expense accounts.

Graham teaches shrewdness, thrift, and plain dealing in a voice full of stockyard humor. The book ran to its sixtieth thousand within months of publication. Readers took the letters as real wisdom from a real merchant king. They remain a funny, quotable primer on American business manners at the century's turn.
21983-the-continental-monthly-vol-4-no-1:
Literature and national policy share this fourth volume of the Continental Monthly, running from July to December 1863 in New York. The index shows a wartime magazine at work: American finances and resources by Robert J. Walker, currency and national finances, and a detective's story for relief. Emancipation in Jamaica opens the volume, arguing from British West Indian figures that freedom had not ruined the islands.

A diary of Frances Krasinska carries Polish life of the last century in monthly parts. Dying in the Hospital speaks from Louisville, close to the war's western edge. The Continental Monthly was founded to give the Union a literary champion. This volume mixes poems, history, and hard money argument in that cause, month by month.
22138-notes-and-queries-number-54-novemb:
Notes and Queries number 54 appeared on November 9, 1850, closing the journal's first full year. The paper's plan was simple: literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists asked and answered in print. One note here concerns Latin hymns sung to marked tunes. A memorandum explains that the Bishop of Ossory composed the songs for his cathedral clergy.

Prefixed lines in the manuscript showed the air each hymn should follow, the note argues. Such details, dry alone, build real knowledge in company. Around them sit the usual queries on books, families, and customs. The issue shows the journal's method working smoothly: print the question, and Britain's scholars will crowd to answer.
22176-the-winged-men-of-orcon-a-complete:
David R. Sparks wrote The Winged Men of Orcon as a complete novelette for the pulp magazines. Far out at the edge of the universe, the blurb says, two scientists play a game of wits with Earth as the prize. The narrator wakes in darkness after a wrecked spaceship. Breathing is hard; the night feels thick as fluid pigment.

He finds keys, frees his handcuffs, and takes up an atomic gun and a cold-ray flashlight. On Orcon he meets the winged men of the title. Sparks piles wonder on danger in the accepted pulp manner. The novelette is pure space adventure from science fiction's first loud decade.
22215-the-frozen-pirate:
W. Clark Russell, the great Victorian writer of the sea, published The Frozen Pirate in 1887. A storm opens the tale, with a livid bank of cloud and wind moaning in gusts. The oldest hands aboard confess they never heard blasts more portentous. The ship is wrecked among icebergs, and the narrator loses his companions one by one.

Alone on an island of ice, he finds a frozen ship and its frozen pirate crew. Thawing brings horror back to life in Russell's famous invention. The tale mixes sea realism with the uncanny. It became one of the best-known short sea novels of its century.
22222-how-to-write-letters-formerly-the-:
Mary Owens Crowther wrote How to Write Letters, first called The Book of Letters, as a complete guide to correct correspondence. The Doubleday edition appeared in 1922. Crowther opens by mocking the old opener "I take my pen in hand." Most writers, she says, attack the paper with one grim thought: to get the thing over with.

Her chapters cover business letters, friendly letters, invitations, and letters of sympathy. Forms, etiquette, and sample letters fill the book. Such manuals stood on every office shelf when letters ran the world. Crowther's survives as a clear record of how Americans of 1922 were taught to be correct, kind, and brief on paper.
22285-an-american-suffragette:
Isaac N. Stevens published An American Suffragette, a novel, in 1911, when the suffrage fight filled the newspapers. His opening crowds a New York pier as a big Cunarder comes in. Among the hundreds waiting stand two groups, the second determined the first shall not get far away. The second group is the press, each man hunting a line from the returning hero, Dr. — the suffragette's famous ally.

Stevens builds his plot on campaigns, speeches, and the comedy of the movement's enemies. The novel sides with the women and argues as it entertains. Such suffrage fiction carried the cause into parlours that no pamphlet reached. It survives as a document of the fight in its final decade.
22339-notes-and-queries-number-66-februa:
Notes and Queries was a weekly exchange for readers with questions. Number 66, dated February 1, 1851, calls itself a medium of intercommunication. Its pages carried notes, queries, and replies from correspondents.

One gratifying letter arrived too late for the week before. The editors lay it before friends, readers, and contributors now. That small notice shows how the journal worked week to week. Readers wrote in; editors sorted, printed, and answered. Over time, such exchanges built a store of facts on history, books, and customs. This single issue preserves the machinery of Victorian curiosity in daily motion.
22624-notes-and-queries-number-52-octobe:
Notes and Queries, number 52, dated October 26, 1850, completes the first year of the beloved British journal of antiquarian exchange. The catalog record names no editor. Its subtitle called it a medium of exchange for literary men, artists, and readers. Its method was simple: print questions, notes, and replies. Then let the learned crowd answer itself.

The editor marks the milestone with pride: every Saturday for twelve months the weekly budget of notes, queries, and replies has reached subscribers. Readers asked about proverbs, old books, family names, and half-remembered verses. Much in the journal still serves genealogists and literary detectives. This anniversary number shows the experiment working, a full year before the formula became an institution.
22625-notes-and-queries-number-67-februa:
Notes and Queries, number 67, dated February 8, 1851, is a weekly number of the British antiquarian journal built on readers' questions and answers. The catalog record names no editor. By its second year the journal had settled into its lasting form: short notes, sharp queries, and replies from scholars across the country.

The sample prints a letter in period spelling, its writer pleading a slow recovery from illness for his failure to keep a promise. He has scarcely been able to get up, or to hold correspondence with friends in town, and awaits papers a king promised to send. Letters like this, half scholarship and half gossip, give the journal its charm. The number preserves research as social exchange.
22779-the-false-chevalier-or-the-lifegua:
The False Chevalier, or The Lifeguard of Marie Antoinette is a historical romance of the French Revolution, built, the author says, on real papers. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its story, the preface explains, rests on a packet of worm-eaten letters. The documents turned up in an old French-Canadian house by the St. Lawrence.

The romance they rudely outline, with its intrigues, brilliant surroundings, and intensity of feeling, fascinated the writer once history and imagination had given it the necessary touches. The result was the present book. A lifeguard of the doomed queen, false names, and revolutionary peril drive the plot. The Canadian frame adds a second mystery: how the papers of Versailles crossed the Atlantic to molder by the great river.
22783-the-new-england-magazine-volume-1-:
The New England Magazine presents volume 1, number 3, dated March 1886, the Bay State magazine's third monthly number. The catalog record names no editor. By its third issue the magazine had settled into its mix of regional description, history, essays, and verse.

The sample paints a Maine river scene in high summer: at the weirs along the river, fishermen pull in nets glimmering with the night's catch. Bustling little tugs struggle nobly against the tide, each towing half a dozen icers. Bathers' merry shouts from Popham Beach mingle with the roar of the incoming tide. Dark pine-clad hills close the view northward. Such set pieces sold the region to itself. The number shows the young magazine painting New England in its best light.
23011-eatin-crow-and-the-best-man-in-gar:
Drinks go round in Eatin' Crow and the Best Man in Garotte, Frank Harris's Western tale. Answering Bent's continued grumbling, Muirhead says pleasantly that things aren't so bad in Garotte. This bar don't look like poverty, he argues, and if he sets up drinks for the crowd, it's because he's glad to be in this camp.

Garotte, a California mining camp, supplies Harris with gamblers, pride, and a title's worth of humiliation to serve someone. Eatin' crow, in frontier slang, means swallowing your words, and the best man here is measured by camp standards. Harris writes the West as a place where reputation is currency. The tale spends that currency briskly, in bars and boasts, toward its reckoning.
23025-the-book-of-business-etiquette:
Nella Henney's Book of Business Etiquette sizes up the businessman himself. Henney finds the businessman picturesque and even lovable. He lacks a knight's dash, she grants. Yet the old human mixture of noble and baser qualities fills him completely.

Around that portrait the manual builds its rules. Letters, interviews, introductions, and office conduct all get their proper forms for the 1920s American workplace. Etiquette here is strategy, a way to be judged well by strangers quickly. The book charms now as a time capsule of the skyscraper age. Its advice on courtesy has aged better than its advice on almost everything else.
241-clotelle-or-the-colored-heroine-a-ta:
William Wells Brown, himself escaped from slavery, wrote one of the first novels by an African American. Clotelle, or the Colored Heroine follows mixed-race women through the Southern social circle, where beauty and bondage meet. Planters' wives, slave women, and quadroon daughters share a corrupted domestic world.

Brown denounces the crime of bondage that produced such families and left no safeguard for virtue. Clotelle's story moves through sale, escape, and the fight for freedom. The novel blends protest, romance, and documentary detail. It stands as a pioneering work of African American fiction.
2760-celebrated-crimes-complete:
Alexandre Dumas, pere, gathers his whole Celebrated Crimes in this complete edition in eight volumes, dated 1910. The contents run from the Borgias and the Cenci through the massacres of the south to the marquise de Brinvilliers and beyond.

Murderers, queens, poisoners, and impostors parade through Renaissance Italy, Reformation France, and revolutionary Europe. Dumas turns trial records and chronicles into vivid narrative, with romantic fire throughout. The set serves as a library of true crime, told by one of fiction's great storytellers. Eight volumes of murder, treason, and poison fill the set.
277-trinity-site:
The United States Department of Energy's National Atomic Museum tells the Trinity story in brief. Trinity Site covers the first atomic test, Jumbo, the Schmidt-McDonald ranch house, notes, and bibliography. The test took place on July 16, 1945, in the final month of World War II.

Conducted by the secret Manhattan Engineer District on the Alamogordo range, Trinity lay about 230 miles south of Los Alamos. The range, once grazing land, is now White Sands Missile Range. The booklet explains the test, the site, and the museum. It serves as a compact official history.
279-photos-and-maps-of-trinity-atomic-te:
This file lists the photographs and maps of the Trinity atomic test site, courtesy of the White Sands Missile Range public affairs office. Each entry names its image: the base camp, the blast at ten seconds, and Oppenheimer and Groves in the crater. The gadget's lift into the hundred-foot tower appears twice.

Other images show Jumbo's unloading, the McDonald-Schmidt ranch house where the plutonium core was assembled, and a Manhattan Project patch. Road maps and a visitor site map complete the set, with the White Sands emblem. The list serves as a caption index to a visual record of July 1945.
29-the-1990-united-states-census-incompl:
Tables from the 1990 Census of Population and Housing fill this partial file. State entries list total population by sex and age, with median age and related counts. The Alabama tables open the sequence shown here.

Readers should note the file's own label: it is incomplete, not the full census release. Even in part, it shows how the Census Bureau broke down each state's people. Researchers use such tables to track age structure and growth state by state. Even partial, the tables help local historians compare towns and counties in that census year.
2988-mark-twain-a-biography-complete:
Albert Bigelow Paine's complete Mark Twain: A Biography gathers the whole personal and literary life of Samuel Langhorne Clemens in one text. Paine dedicates the work to Clara Clemens Gabrilowitsch, who upheld his purpose to write history rather than eulogy, and thanks Howells, Twichell, and Goodman for years of help. The biography runs from Clemens's Missouri childhood through his world fame.

Later chapters follow Twain onto the amateur stage, playing Peter Spuyk in The Loan of a Lover at Hartford on April 26, 1876, with Helen Smith as Gertrude. Paine notes genuine dramatic talent in the Hartford company. The complete text lets readers follow one life without hunting across volumes, from river pilot to beloved author.
3124-the-people-for-whom-shakespeare-wro:
Warner rebuilds the London audience that first watched Shakespeare, starting on the morning Elizabeth died, 24 March 1603. Sir Robert Cary rides unsent to tell James of Scotland, and the new king scatters knighthoods as he travels south, making twenty-eight at Theobald's alone. The anecdote sets the tone: a restless, rank-hungry, talkative England crowding into playhouses.

The essay then asks what such people brought to the plays: their habits, their news, their taste for bold speech and quick action. By sketching the crowd before the stage, Warner helps a modern reader hear Shakespeare's lines as his own hearers heard them, amid the noise and appetite of a capital changing monarchs.
3253-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
This complete constitutional edition gathers Abraham Lincoln's papers and writings in full. Arthur Brooks Lapsley edited the set, with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt. An essay on Lincoln by Carl Schurz and an address on Lincoln by Joseph Choate join the edition. The volumes run from early speeches to the presidency's final papers.

Volume one opens just after Lincoln's re-election, with an offhand speech to serenaders on the evening of 10 November 1864. It has long been a grave question, he begins, in his plain, careful way. Lincoln whole, in order, from early speeches to final papers: that is the set's plain promise, and it keeps it.
3259-countess-kate:
Charlotte M Yonge tells the story of Countess Kate in this 1902 Macmillan volume, joined with The Stokesley Secret. A frontispiece shows a man comforting a little girl on the stairs while a boy watches. That scene fixes the book's temper: a child in need of kindness, watched over by older eyes. Kate herself is the young countess of the title.

Yonge, a favorite Victorian writer for girls, builds her tale on rank, duty, and affection. A child lifted by a title must learn what the title obliges her to be. Rank, duty, and affection test a child lifted by a title, and kindness does the teaching.
3306-at-suvla-bay-being-the-notes-and-sk:
John Hargrave, White Fox of The Scout, served with the 32nd Field Ambulance, X Division, in the Mediterranean Expeditionary Force. His notes and sketches of the Dardanelles campaign, written at Suvla Bay during the Great War, make this book. A dedication verse sets the contrast: the author and Minobi once played at Ali Baba on a green linoleum floor, and now camp near Lala Baba by the blue Aegean shore.

Hargrave sailed, as his verse says, in the good ship Argo to a war that was no game. The sketches that follow mix humor and horror at the front: wounded men, officers, and the daily grind of a failed landing. The book preserves a young ambulance man's Gallipoli, told while the campaign was still fresh and its outcome still in doubt.
3350-the-wandering-jew-complete:
This file holds Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew complete, in a single text. A note on the author opens it: Sue lived from 1804 to 1857, and his path to fiction was unusual. Physicians and seamen have often made novelists, the note says, but rarely has one man trained in both callings won his greatest fame as a writer. Sue began as a physician and surgeon, then spent six years in the French Navy.

The novel that followed made him famous across Europe. A wandering outcast, a scattered family, and a Jesuit scheme for a vast inheritance drive its thousand pages. Readers who want Sue whole, without hunting through eleven separate volumes, will find the entire serial here, from its Paris opening to its final reckoning.
3389-literature-and-life-complete:
William Dean Howells gathers his thoughts on books, travel, and daily life in this full collection of essays. The table of contents runs from his defense of literature as a part of life to pieces on a Dutch hotel and Spanish prisoners of war. It also covers a summer colony and the streets of New York. Short stories and sketches sit beside longer critical essays, so the book shifts tone often.

What holds the mix together is Howells's plain, observant voice. He writes about a circus in the suburbs, a dime museum, a beach at Rockaway, and a horse show with the same care he gives to famous authors. The collection works as an introduction to his nonfiction and as a portrait of American life at the turn of the century.
3567-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-compl:
Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne tells his full story of Napoleon in this complete edition of his memoirs, edited by Colonel R W Phipps in 1891. The contents run from prefaces for the 1836 and 1885 editions through volume one, covering 1769 to 1800, and on through the Consulate, the empire, and the fall. Bourrienne served as Napoleon's private secretary and knew him from youth.

No other single source gives so long an inside view of Napoleon's daily life, orders, and conversations. Readers should remember that Bourrienne writes as a former friend with his own grievances, so his judgments need care. Still, as a record of how power looked from the next desk, the memoirs remain essential reading on Napoleon.
3580-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant, Napoleon's first valet, tells the whole story of the emperor's private life in this complete edition, translated by Walter Clark in 1895. The preface notes that the work first appeared in French in 1830 and had never before been rendered into English, with the original volumes nearly out of print. The translator added notes, and the publishers added illustrations.

Constant's aim, in his own phrase, was to paint Caesar in undress: to show Napoleon at home, at table, and on campaign, away from state portraits. Readers get the full arc, from the Consulate household to abdication and farewell. The complete volume suits readers who want the valet's view in one place, without hunting through twelve separate parts.
3600-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-compl:
This complete edition gathers all of Montaigne's Essays, from the prefatory life and letters through Books One, Two, and Three. The preface presents Montaigne as a great French writer who deserves to rank as a classic in all countries, not only in his own land. His essays, the preface says, made his intellectual and physical self public property, as he took the world into his confidence on every subject.

Readers get the full range in one volume: custom, fear, friendship, cannibals, books, vanity, and experience. Montaigne studies himself to study mankind, and his digressions became a model for the essay ever after. The complete edition suits readers ready to live with Montaigne at length, dipping in or reading straight through.
3649-the-dwelling-place-of-light-complet:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, tells the full story of Janet Bumpus and her mill town in this complete edition. The novel opens with a glacier image for industrial life, as helpless people are torn from the parent rock, crushed, and left stranded in strange places. Edward Bumpus, Janet's father, is severed from the firm granite of stable things and cast into a shifting world.

The complete story follows Janet from childhood through work, love, and political awakening, as strikes and speeches shake Hampton. Churchill writes a large novel of labor, faith, and class in New England. The complete edition suits readers who want the whole arc in one volume, from family loss to a young woman's stand.
3664-yvette:
Guy de Maupassant writes a novella about Yvette, a young woman in Paris society, and the men who circle her. The chapters are called The Initiation of Saval, Bougival and Love, Enlightenment, and From Emotion to Philosophy. The story opens as Jean de Servigny and Leon Saval leave the Cafe Riche on a fine night, choosing to walk rather than take a cab.

Saval, a newcomer to Yvette's world, learns its rules at Bougival and in Paris drawing rooms, where charm covers calculation. Maupassant writes with his usual irony about love, money, and reputation. The novella suits readers who enjoy his short fiction: a sharp, sad portrait of a girl whose beauty opens doors that lead nowhere kind.
3684-mr-crewe-s-career-complete:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, tells the full career of Mr Crewe in this complete edition. The story begins with Hilary Vane of Ripton, a lawyer, deacon, and trustee who boasts he never held office, yet whose word moves the state. Against Vane's quiet machine stands Crewe, a young reformer who desires only to make his state a utopia.

The complete novel follows Crewe from rallies and newspapers through legislative hearings to the test of his ideals in office. Churchill writes New Hampshire politics as a contest between friendship, interest, and principle. The complete edition suits readers who want the whole political story in one volume, from portrait to climax.
3739-a-far-country-complete:
Winston Churchill's full novel of modern America follows Hugh Paret from boyhood to middle age in one long arc. The book opens with Hugh calling himself a corporation lawyer by accident and promising an autobiography of a romanticist. It then tracks him through school, the law, railroad politics, sudden wealth, and a marriage strained by ambition, until success itself stands trial.

Readers get the whole story here rather than in parts, with the Hutchins family, their library, and their riverside houses marking each stage of the rise. Churchill keeps the moral question in view throughout, asking what a life spent getting is worth. The complete text suits readers who want to judge Hugh whole, from his first hopes to his final reckoning.
3766-coniston-complete:
Winston Churchill's full Coniston novel tells a New Hampshire love story against the rise of machine politics. The book opens after Jackson's presidency with the Boss Era. It follows Cynthia Ware from childhood errands at the village store to womanhood at Miss Sadler's school. It also tracks Jethro Bass as he builds a political machine from favors, railroads, and loyal hounds like Jake Wheeler. Love, loyalty, and conscience pull Cynthia between Jethro's world and Bob Worthington's.

The complete text lets readers judge the whole design, from the tannery house years to the Boston parlors where Cynthia renounces and reconsiders. Churchill's moral stays constant, that popular rule is only as good as the virtue of its people. The novel suits readers who want one long American chronicle rather than a tale in parts.
3775-napoleon-bonaparte:
John Abbott wrote this popular life of Napoleon for readers who wanted the whole career in one stirring volume. The book follows the Corsican boy to Toulon, Egypt, and the coup that made him First Consul, then through Austerlitz, Jena, and the Russian snows to exile and Saint Helena. Abbott favors vivid scenes over dry analysis, with camps, courts, and battlefields drawn in warm, admiring colors.

A Spanish interlude shows the method, as a ragged stranger with a carbine eats a priest's whole supper and drinks to his host's health before the war resumes. The biography is partisan and old fashioned, but it carries a reader swiftly across twenty years of European upheaval. Those who want a first life of Napoleon, full of incident, will find Abbott a genial guide.
3824-the-lamp-of-fate:
Margaret Pedler opens this family romance at Coverdale, where Hugh Vallincourt waits for news of a son and heir. For eight successive generations the first born of the Vallincourts has been a boy, so fixed a habit that no one doubts the ninth will follow suit. The house lies silent with disinfectant in the air, and hushed steps move upstairs while Hugh stares at lawns and leafless trees.

Later chapters carry the story to Devon lanes, where a boy called Coppertop rides a wagonette toward Storran of Stockleigh, past drivers who swish whips more at flies than at horses. Pedler asks what lamp guides children stumbling in the dark, quoting Omar Khayyam for her title. Readers who like generational sagas will find fate, family, and romance woven together.
3854-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
This complete text gathers all seven books of Madame de Montespan's memoirs of the court of Louis the Fourteenth. The translator's preface asks for a fairer hearing than harsh historians gave her. The memoirs were compiled in a vague, desultory way, with no regard for chronological order. Their value lies in self portraiture, as a cynical court lady whose beauty bewitched a king and whose sarcasm cut duchesses describes her own rise and fall.

War scenes balance the gossip, with orders to ravage Liege and Juliers, families in flight, castles sacked, and convents in flames, while Spanish and Dutch leaders rouse the people to resist. The complete memoirs suit readers who want the whole arc, from favorite to exile, in the favorite's own sharp voice.
3900-court-memoirs-of-france-series-comp:
This vast file binds the whole court memoir series into one reading text of nearly eight million characters. Its contents list Marguerite de Valois, Cardinal de Retz, Madame de Montespan, and the Duchesse d'Orleans on Louis the Fourteenth. Saint-Simon, du Hausset, Campan, the Saint Cloud letters, and the Count de Grammont complete the set. Three centuries of French courts, from Valois queens to Napoleon's upstarts, stand in a single sequence.

A supper scene gives the flavor, as the Duke de Berry arrives to salute the king at table, all hearts open, and talk turns to post horses and roads. Readers who want the complete run, rather than single volumes, will find a library in one file, best dipped into by reign or by memoirist, since no one reads it straight through.
3918-serge-panine-complete:
This complete text gives all of Georges Ohnet's Serge Panine, crowned by the French Academy, with a general introduction to the series by Gaston Boissier's circle. The editor's preface presents the French Immortals as great romances since 1784. They are offered to American readers as a window on the inner life of a people whose greatness no turn of fortune could dim. Ohnet's novel of wealth, marriage, and speculation follows in full.

A ballroom passage shows its gossip machinery. Le Brede asks who a rich cousin of the Prince may be, and learns she owns a district in London and was kind to Serge Panine a year earlier. Her husband, shut in a Scottish castle and out of his mind, explains why she never married the Prince. Readers who want the whole novel will find ambition, ruin, and drawing room talk complete.
3922-the-red-lily-complete:
This complete text gives all of Anatole France's The Red Lily, with a preface on the author's life. Jacques Anatole Thibault, born in Paris in 1844 to a bookseller of the Quai Malaquais, was educated at College Stanislas, published poetry in the 1870s, and joined the French Academy in 1896. His critical writings fill four volumes of La Vie Litteraire, and his political articles fill Opinions Sociales.

The novel itself follows Therese through Florence, where morning thoughts dwell on walks, Virgins framed with angels, and children painted or carved who sing the Alleluia of grace. In the Brancacci chapel, her lover talks of Masaccio so vividly that she seems to see the adolescent master of masters. Readers who want France whole will find irony, art, and adultery in one long narrative.
3926-monsieur-madame-and-be-be-complete:
This complete text gives all of Gustave Droz's Monsieur, Madame and Bebe, the sketches crowned by the Academy in 1866. The preface traces Droz from Paris birth in 1832, son of sculptor Jules Antoine Droz, through the Beaux Arts and the Salon of 1857. From painting he turned to authorship under the name Gustave Z in La Vie Parisienne. His articles won favor as the work of an exquisite raconteur and sharp observer of intimate family life.

A domestic scene shows his method. A mother examines an embroidered garment, calls it lovely, and is interrupted by a knock and several voices, among them aunt Laura, a godmother, and Madame de P. with her thick lips ready for cheeks. Their glittering, ferreting looks intimidate the narrator. Readers who want Droz whole will find bachelor and married life in one comic volume.
3930-prince-zilah-complete:
This complete text gives all of Jules Claretie's Prince Zilah, with a preface by the Comte d'Haussonville of the French Academy. The preface calls Claretie the king of the chronicle, born at Limoges in 1840, educated at the Lycee Bonaparte, and destined for commerce before newspapers claimed him. Under names like Olivier de Jalin, Perdican, and Candide, he wrote for the Diogene, La France, L'Illustration, the Figaro, and the Rappel, and entered the Academy in 1888.

The novel's midnight scene shows its romantic machinery, as a Muscovite girl quiets hounds baying in the Himalayas kennel, unfastens their chains, and sends them bounding over the lawn in pale moonlight. She retraces her steps with the indifference her father might show ordering a spy shot. Readers who want Zilah whole will find Hungary, Paris, and a fate sealed by letters.
3934-zibeline-complete:
This file holds the whole of Philippe de Massa's Zibeline, with a life of its author. Alexandre Philippe Regnier de Massa, Marquis de Massa, was born in Paris in 1831. He took a cavalry commission after Saint Cyr, served in the Imperial Guards, and fought in the Italian and Franco German wars. He later wrote plays, a ballet with Petipa, and this brilliant romance of 1892.

A comic passage shows its machinery, as the actress Eugenie tells how Monsieur Desvanneaux announced her for a charity kermess. Under the mantle of charity, she says, the holy man paid court to her.
