Fanning sets out their privileges, including rights of nominating and presenting candidates, which in many places were still in force when he wrote.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comtesse-de-l:
Pierre Marique's entry follows the Comtesse de La Fayette, memoirist and novelist, born at Paris in 1634, dead in 1693. She knew Latin and Italian, taught partly by Menage. Wit and talent won her Paris's lead. With the Marquise de Sévigné, she embodied Les Précieuses, who shaped Louis XIV's young court. Friends included Condé, Huet, La Rochefoucauld, Bossuet, La Fontaine.

She was confidante of Princess Henrietta, the king's sister-in-law. Her first novel, La Princesse de Montpensier, appeared unsigned in 1662. Zayde followed in 1670; her masterpiece La Princesse de Clèves in 1678 pictures Fronde society in sixteenth-century scenes. Its moral beauty recalls Corneille; it counts as the first French psychological novel. Clear and lively, its style avoids vulgar words, the one Précieuse trace. Her court memoirs for 1688, 1689 close the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curate:
This entry explains the curate, from the Latin for care, as one charged with the cure, or care, of souls. The Church of England still uses it in that broad sense, and the French cure denotes a parish priest. In English-speaking countries, however, curate has come to mean an assistant priest, sent by the bishop to help the rector or parish priest.

Technically the parish priest holds the cure, while his helpers are vicars and coadjutors, but the entry uses curate in its accepted English sense. It traces the office from the early Church, when each diocese had one church in the bishop's city, through growth that multiplied churches and priests in city and country. The standing and duties of English curates are treated with legal references.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-amelote: An entry on Denis Amelote, a French Oratorian born at Saintes in 1609 who died in Paris in 1678. Ordained in 1631 and a doctor of the Sorbonne, he gave French readers a New Testament translation in four volumes, issued between 1666 and 1670, that was prized and often reprinted. Most of his other Scripture works draw on that edition, and he also wrote in defence of papal rulings against the Jansenists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desire-raoul-:
A life of Désiré Raoul Rochette, a French archaeologist born at Saint-Amand in 1789 who died in Paris in 1854. After classical study at Bourges and the École Normale, he took a grammar chair at Louis-le-Grand in 1810 and married the sculptor Houdon's daughter. An Institute prize for a memoir on Greek colonies came in 1813, and in 1815 he succeeded Guizot in the Sorbonne chair of modern history.

Election to the Academy of Inscriptions followed in 1816, then a keepership of medals and antiques in 1818. A censor's post in 1820 turned students against him and stalled his lectures. He moved to the archaeology chair in 1824, and became perpetual secretary of the Academy of Fine Arts in 1839. Books on Greek colonies, the Cimmerian Bosphorus, Pompeii, and archaeology itself anchor his output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-francis:
Diego Francisco Aduarte was a Dominican missionary and historian born at Saragossa in 1566. He sailed for the Philippines in 1594 and landed at Manila the next year. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry singles out his work among the Chinese residents of the islands, where his preaching met with rare success.

Voyages to Siam and Cochin China in aid of native rulers brought hunger, thirst, and danger from treacherous hosts. Yet he pressed on for years by sea and land. His History of the Province of the Holy Rosary, printed at Manila in 1634, remains the entry's centerpiece, a rare chronicle of the Dominican missions of the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dionysius-the:
Dionysius the Areopagite is usually taken to be the judge of the Areopagus whom Saint Paul converted at Athens. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry untangles two great errors that grew around his name. First, a set of famous mystical writings was ascribed to him, though they came from a later hand. Second, he was popularly matched with Saint Denis, the first bishop of Paris and martyr of Gaul.

The entry sets aside the Paris legend and takes up the writer himself, his works, and their fate across the ages. It sorts the writings, weighs their contents and character, and traces how they were handed down. Readers meet a shadowy author whose books shaped medieval thought far beyond what his true name could claim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingo-ferna:
Domingo Fernandez Navarrete was a Dominican missionary and archbishop born about 1610 at Penafiel in Old Castile. He took the habit about 1630 and was offered chairs of Thomist theology at several Spanish universities. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he turned them down to preach to the heathen. He sailed in 1646 with twenty-seven brethren by way of Mexico to the Philippines, landing there in June 1648.

He taught theology at the Dominican University of Saint Thomas in Manila, then went to China in 1657. After learning the tongue he labored chiefly in Fo-kien until persecution broke out in 1665. Forbidden to preach, he wrote instead, leaving historical, political, and religious treatises on China and a Chinese catechism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donato-braman:
Donato Bramante, also called d'Agnolo for his father Angelo, was an Italian architect and painter born about 1444 at Monte Asdrualdo. He died at Rome on 11 March 1514. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that little is known of his youth and that Vasari erred often about his early growth. Scholars now fairly agree that Laurana, who built Urbino's ducal palace, pointed him toward the High Renaissance.

His work falls into two periods, Milan first and Rome after. Milan shows a picturesque, decorative manner, while Rome shows the purer High Renaissance style in works as perfect as their age allowed. The entry cites Geymuller on his first plans for Saint Peter's, the crown of his Roman years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durham-rite:
The Durham Rite is known first from the Ritual of the Church of Durham, also called the Ritual of King Aelfrith. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry dates the manuscript to the early ninth century and keeps it in the Durham cathedral library. It holds chapters, chants, and above all collects from Epiphany to Easter, then a proper and a common of saints, with many forms for blessings. Most of it bears an interlinear Anglo-Saxon translation.

Blank pages later gained hymns, exorcisms, and a list of contractions from canon law books, added by later scribes. The entry traces the rite's links to Durham and prints related texts from the Surtees Society. For students of old English worship, it opens a service book written when Northumbria still prayed in two tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-east-syrian-r:
The East Syrian Rite, also called Chaldean, Assyrian, or Persian, serves Nestorians and Eastern Catholic bodies across Syria, Mesopotamia, Persia, and Malabar. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the name Chaldean, which in Syriac meant magician, but in European tongues came to mean Syrian nationality and the Syriac tongue. Seventeenth-century Latin missionaries at Mosul attached the name to East Syrian Catholics, distinguishing them from West Syrians and Nestorians.

The entry traces the rite's history and its liturgy, down to the consecration of altars. There the whole altar is anointed with fresh olive oil blessed by the bishop, not oil of the holy horn. Four consecration crosses mark the sanctuary walls. It offers a full portrait of a rite that bridges East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edme-mariotte:
Edme Mariotte was a French physicist and priest, born at Dijon about 1620 and dead at Paris in 1684. Ordained to the priesthood, he was made prior of Saint-Martin-sous-Beaune near Dijon in reward for his work in science. He belonged to the Royal Society of Science from its start in 1666, and his collected works came out at Leyden in 1717.

His name lives on through the gas law of 1676. It first appeared in an essay on air. At a fixed heat, the bulk of a gas shrinks as the weight pressing on it grows. The entry also covers his tests on water pressure, the swing of weights, the flow of water, and his flask for a steady stream. It sketches a man who trusted careful trial, doubt, and plain rules of thought over guesswork.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-white:
Edward White was an Irish emigrant whose family left a mark on American Catholic life, born in County Limerick late in the eighteenth century and dead in December 1863. Early in the nineteenth century he crossed to America and settled at Binghamton in New York. There he founded and ran a school for young women, which lasted from 1830 until his wife's death in 1851.

White had nine children. Five of his daughters entered religious orders, the best known being Madame Catherine White of the Religious of the Sacred Heart, who wrote school books on mythology, classical literature, and church history. His eldest son James became a prominent lawyer in New York City. The entry is a short family record, valued chiefly for the children it names.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emmanuel-sche:
Emmanuel Schelstrate was a Belgian theologian, born at Antwerp in 1649 and dead at Rome in 1692. While canon of Antwerp Cathedral he was called to Rome by Innocent IX and made assistant librarian of the Vatican Library. A fine scholar in early church history, he became the accredited defender of papal supremacy, which is why his writings have often been judged harshly.

His Antiquitas Illustrata of 1678 gathers papal decrees and church history, and in it he attacked Launoy's errors on the primacy of Rome. He planned a larger second edition but issued only two volumes, in 1692 and 1697. He disputed with Arnauld and Maimbourg over councils and popes, opposed the Gallican clergy's declaration of 1682, and wrote on the origin of the Anglican Church against Stillingfleet, Dean of Saint Paul's. He published many other works besides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eustathius-of:
Eustathius of Sebaste, born about 300 and dead about 377, was one of the chief founders of monastic life in Asia Minor and for years the close friend of Saint Basil. Son of Eulalius, Bishop of Sebaste, he studied under Arius, was ordained priest, and founded a community of monks whose strict ways drew censure. A synod at Gangra about 340 condemned his followers for forbidding marriage, shunning married priests, fasting on Sundays while skipping appointed fast days, and claiming special grace for their own meetings.

He became Bishop of Sebaste about 356, and Basil, then learning the monastic life, admired and defended him for years. But Eustathius wavered all his life between forms of Arianism, signed contradictory formulas, and at last led the Pneumatomachians, who denied that the Holy Ghost shares the same substance as the Father. Basil broke with him about 372.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fate:
Fate means an unseen power fixing the course of events in advance. Catholics prefer providence for God's rule and natural law for fixed physical order. The Greeks pictured fate as Moira, or three sisters named Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos. Romans matched them with their own Parcae, or Fata.

Thinkers sought a cause for events that seemed to follow no law. Some turned to the stars, supposing heavenly bodies shaped earthly fortunes. The Stoics made fate universal, while Epicureans denied it through the atoms' swerve. Catholic teaching holds God's decree firm, yet never predetermines the abuse of free will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerard-groote:
Gerard Groote, who founded the Brethren of the Common Life, turned from rich prebends to devout poverty. Born at Deventer in 1340, he studied at Aachen and the Sorbonne in medicine, theology, and canon law. He taught at Deventer's chapter school in 1362 and carried a secret mission to Urban V at Avignon. At Cologne he taught philosophy and theology on two prebends and ample means.

Meeting his Sorbonne fellow Henry of Calcar, prior of Munnikhuizen, Groote stripped himself of honors and goods. He spent three years in retreat there under Ruysbroek's influence and emerged a preacher with diaconate and licence for Utrecht. Youths flocked to him, and with his disciple Florence Radewyns he founded the Brethren at Zwolle to work, pray, and copy good books together. His fearless attacks on vice cost him his licence, though he appealed to the pope. He died of pestilence caught ministering to the sick in 1384.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-nacch:
Giacomo Nacchiante, also called Naclantus, was a Dominican theologian born at Florence, who died at Chioggia in 1569. He studied at Bologna beside Michael Ghislieri, the future Pius V, and later taught philosophy and theology in Rome. Paul III made him Bishop of Chioggia in 1544. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his career through the Council of Trent and the doubts it raised about him.

At Trent he protested the fourth session's decree that church traditions be received with the same reverence as Scripture. He then gave reverent assent once the great assembly had confirmed it. Later doubts about his orthodoxy faded, the article says, because Pius IV trusted him with grave affairs. His works, printed at Venice in 1567, include commentaries on Ephesians and Romans, a marrow of Scripture, and treatises in theology and metaphysics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gil-vicente:
Gil Vicente was a Portuguese dramatist born about 1470, who was still living in 1536. He left the study of law for literature, and his humorous lyrics appear in Garcia de Resende's Cancioneiro. A Catholic Encyclopedia article styles him, with good reason, the father of the Portuguese drama, on the strength of no fewer than forty-two plays.

Ten of his pieces are in Spanish, fourteen in Portuguese, and the rest mix the two tongues. Many were written for religious and national festivals or for events in the royal family, while others aimed only at entertainment. His first play, Visitacao, celebrated the birth of John III in 1502. Court ladies and gentlemen acted beside him in palace performances, and his seventeen religious autos, the Obras de devocao, show a genuinely devout Catholic at work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hakodate:
Japan's northern diocese of Hakodate covers six provinces of northern Nippon with Yezo, the Kuriles, and southern Saghalin. It holds about nine million people, including 17,000 Ainu, the last remnant of the islands' first population. A vicariate from April 1891 and a diocese that June, it was entrusted to the Paris Foreign Missions, with twenty-four missionaries, one Japanese priest, and twenty residences by 1908.

Sixteenth-century Christianity survives only in crosses and images hidden in families and pagoda treasuries, and present Catholics are converts, mostly won before 1895, when faith still seemed the ground of civilization. Materialism and national pride have since made conversions rare, yet 345 adults were baptized in 1908. The writer expects the Japanese, lovers of truth who admire Catholic order and self-sacrifice, to come in numbers yet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-digby-b:
Henry Digby Beste, born at Lincoln in 1768, was educated at Magdalen College, Oxford, took Anglican deacon's orders in 1791, and preached at Lincoln. Doubts about the Established Church's spiritual authority, deepened by conversation with the Abbé Beaumont, led to his reception into the Catholic Church in 1798. His early writings defended Christianity against French philosophers and republicans and argued for priestly absolution in terms later Tractarians claimed.

After his conversion Beste contributed to Catholic periodicals, travelled for years in France and Italy, and wrote books on his family's residence abroad that open with an account of his own conversion. Cardinal Wiseman met him at Rome during the Jubilee of 1825. His last work, Poverty and the Baronet's Family, a Catholic story, appeared ten years after his death at Brighton in 1836, closing a literary life shaped by one great change of allegiance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignacio-de-ir:
Ignacio de Iriarte was a Spanish painter, born at Azcoitia in Guipuzcoa in 1620 and dead at Seville in 1685. Son of Esteban de Iriarte and Magdalena Zabala, he was schooled at home, then went to Seville in 1642 and entered the elder Herrera's studio. There he learned colouring, but he never drew the human figure with spirit or accuracy.

He therefore gave himself exclusively to landscape, the one Spanish artist to walk that rarely trodden path and win the greatest celebrity in it. Settling near the mountains at Aracena in 1646, he married twice. He joined Seville's Academy as a founding member and its first secretary in 1660, and worked intimately with Murillo, who painted figures while Iriarte painted the landscape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ippolito-pind:
Verona poet Ippolito Pindemonte, born 13 November 1753 and dead there 18 November 1828, was schooled at the Collegio di San Carlo in Modena. Wide travel in Italy and abroad gave him a broad circle of literary friends, and he watched the Revolution begin in Paris, turning that shock into his poem Francia. London, Berlin, and Vienna followed before he returned to Verona in 1791.

His health was broken and his hopes for Italy's renewal and greatness had failed, so his last years went to study and religious practice. His chief works are the Poesie and Prose campestri, published between 1788 and 1794. They also include the Sepolcri and a version of the Odyssey. Alla Luna, Alla Salute, La Melanconia, and La Giovinezza rank among the most admired pieces. The entry sketches a gentle poet of loss and landscape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-spencer:
James Spencer Northcote was born at Feniton Court in Devonshire on 26 May 1821 and died at Stoke-upon-Trent in Staffordshire on 3 March 1907. George Barons Northcote counted him as his second son, in an old Devonshire family of Norman descent. His first schooling came at Ilmington Grammar School, and he won a scholarship to Corpus Christi College, Oxford, in 1837, where Newman shaped his thinking. He took his B.A. in 1841, and in 1842 he married his cousin Susannah Spencer Ruscombe Poole.

Orders in the Anglican Church in 1844 gave him a curacy at Ilfracombe. He gave it up when his wife joined the Catholic Church in 1845. In 1846 he himself became a Catholic, received at Prior Park College, where he stayed on as a master for a while. From June 1852 to September 1854 he edited the Rambler. After his wife died in 1853, he put himself to writing Catholic school histories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-parisot-:
Jean Parisot de La Valette, forty-eighth grand master of the Knights of Saint John, was born in 1494 and died in Malta in 1568. From an old southern French family, he joined the order young as a knight of Provence, and after Rhodes fell in 1522 followed it to Malta in 1530.

La Valette first campaigned against Barbary corsairs, governed Tripoli from 1537 with firm discipline, and was chosen grand master in 1557. He reasserted order authority over German and Venetian provinces, and devoted his last years to fortifying Malta against the Turks. The capital Valletta, founded after the great siege, bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jephte:
Jephthah, one of Israel's judges, is the subject of this entry drawn from Judges chapters eleven and twelve. A warrior of Gilead and son of a harlot, he was driven from his father's house by half-brothers and fled to Tob in eastern Syria. There he led a band of needy men and raiders.

When Ammonites invaded Gilead's land east of Jordan, the elders begged Jephthah back as their chief, promising him lasting rule if he won. He bargained at length with Ammon's king over land rights, then vowed that whoever first met him on his return home would be offered to the Lord. Victory brought him home to that terrible vow and its fulfilment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lydgate:
John Lydgate was a prolific English poet of the fifteenth century, monk of Bury St. Edmunds and court poet to Henry VI. Born at Lydgate in Suffolk about 1370, he entered Bury abbey at fifteen, was ordained in 1397, and may have studied at Oxford and Cambridge and traveled in France and perhaps Italy. He opened a school, probably at Bury, for sons of the nobility.

His verses were much in request among noble lords and ladies, and he wrote a ballad for Henry VI's coronation, serving eleven years as prior of Hatfield Broadoak from 1423. Ritson numbers 251 poems, including the Troy Book of thirty thousand lines, the Falls of Princes, the Story of Thebes, the Life of Our Lady, and the Dance of Death. Critics agree his work never rises much above mediocrity, yet admirers from Chatterton to Gray praised his careful phrasing and smooth verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-patrick-:
John Patrick Crichton-Stuart, third Marquess of Bute, was a Scottish nobleman, scholar, and munificent patron of Catholic causes. Born at Mountstuart in 1847, only child of the second marquess, he succeeded at six months old and lost his mother in 1859. He was educated at Harrow and Christ Church, Oxford, where advanced Anglican tenets struck his logical mind as inconsistent with separation from Rome.

Received into the Church by Monsignor Capel in December 1868 and confirmed by Pius IX, he attended part of the Vatican Council and traveled in the East. He settled on his vast Scottish and Welsh estates. The first modern peer to hold municipal office, he served as Mayor of Cardiff and twice as Provost of Rothesay. He lavished his Cardiff wealth on poor Catholic missions and impecunious scholars, and served as Lord Rector of Saint Andrews, dying in 1900.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joliette:
Joliette is a Canadian diocese erected by Pius X in 1904 from the Archdiocese of Montreal. It covers the counties of Joliette, Berthier, and Montcalm with four parishes of L'Assomption. It forms a rectangle about 105 miles long by 45 wide, with a population of 63,500 souls, only 1,200 of them non-Catholic.

The diocese counts thirty-eight canonically erected parishes and four with resident priests, served by 115 priests, 104 secular and 11 religious, with 134 religious men and 390 women. Its parishes support the Third Order of St. Francis, the League of the Sacred Heart, Marian congregations, confraternities of Carmel, the Rosary, and the Holy Angels, daily adoration, the Way of the Cross, the St. Vincent de Paul Society, and a temperance society in every parish, while schools include a seminary, commercial colleges and academies, boarding schools, and model schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-antonio-:
Jose Antonio Alzate was a Mexican priest and the most zealous student of the liberal sciences in New Spain. Born at Ozumba in 1738 and dying in 1799, he wrote more than thirty treatises on astronomy, physics, meteorology, antiquities, and metallurgy. He also studied industry, including silk-growing in Mexico, ammonia against mine gases, and maps of New Spain.

Often opposed and even reviled at home, he was made a corresponding member of the French Academy of Sciences, and viceroys and archbishops entrusted him with scientific missions. In 1768 he founded Mexico's Diario Literario and gave the first published notice of the ruins of Xochicalco. He commented on Clavigero's work on aboriginal Mexico and its natural history, making him a pioneer of Mexican science.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-fernande:
Juan Fernández Navarrete was the Spanish painter called el Mudo and the Spanish Titian. Born at Logroño in 1526, he lost his hearing at three and with it his speech. The Hieronymites of Estrella taught him art, and he made his wants known in swift black-and-white sketches. Under Titian in Venice he mastered color.

Made painter to Philip II in 1568, Navarrete decorated the Escorial, where his Nativity of 1575 glows with three lights, brightest from the Child. A Holy Family with a cat, dog, and partridge drew the king's order never to add such indecorous things again. Lope de Vega wrote after his death in 1579 that no face he painted was dumb.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-the-ap:
Julian the Apostate was the Roman emperor who tried to restore paganism. Born at Constantinople in 331, son of Julius Constantius, he survived the massacre of his kin after Constantine's death and was raised under Christian tutors. Resentment at the murders turned him against Christians, and at Nicomedia he gave himself to Neo-Platonic philosophy, magic, and mystery rites.

Named Caesar in 355, Julian won fame in Gaul, routing over thirty thousand Alamanni near Strasbourg and reopening the Rhine. As emperor from 361 to 363, he favored Hellenism and was initiated at Eleusis. He died on 26 June 363, after a reign of less than two years that failed to turn the empire from Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juste:
Juste was the conventional name of Italian sculptors really called Betti. From San Martino a Mensola, near Florence, the first two known members, Giusto and Andrea, never left Italy. Andrea's three sons, Anthony, Andrew, and John, emigrated early to France as leading carriers of Italian Renaissance art beyond the Alps. By 1504 the brothers were at Dol in Brittany, carving Bishop Thomas James's monument.

John, the most illustrious of the house, worked in the Tours workshop of Michel Colombe, last master of the Dijon school. There he blended Flemish realism with French delicacy into a flexible style of his own. Francis I then gave the brothers the Louis XII mausoleum at St-Denis, a work of nearly fifteen years. Its famous contrast pairs the kneeling king above with his naked, wasted corpse below, a new departure in French tomb design.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-king-canute:
Canute the Great (about 994-1035) ruled England, Denmark, and Norway. The son of Sweyn of Denmark, he sailed with his father's invasion fleet. The Danes hailed him king after Sweyn's sudden death in February 1014, though the witan recalled the exiled Athelred instead.

Driven off, Canute returned with a fleet said to number two hundred ships and fought a string of bloody battles, crowned by Assandun, where the English nobility was wiped out. Peace on the Isle of Olney split the kingdom with Edmund Ironside, whose death a month later left Canute sole ruler. In July 1017 he married Emma, Edmund's widow, and fixed the succession on children of that marriage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-salette:
La Salette, in the Grenoble diocese, is famed as the spot where the Blessed Virgin is said to have appeared to two young shepherds, drawing pilgrims ever since. On 19 September 1846, in bright sun on a mountain near the village, Melanie Calvat, fifteen, and Maximin Giraud, eleven, saw a shining beautiful lady.

Speaking French and local patois by turns, she charged them to carry a message to all her people. She warned of chastisement for impiety and promised mercy for amendment. She gave each child a secret. Bishop Philibert de Bruillard's commission accepted the apparition's reality, and cures followed. On 16 November 1851 he declared it certain and allowed the cult of Our Lady of La Salette. Opposition in Grenoble and Lyons raged on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-legate:
A legate, from Latin legare, to send, is in the broad sense anyone sent by another for a representative office. In church usage it means one the pope sends to sovereigns, governments, bishops, or faithful of a country as his representative. He treats church business or even a mission of honour.

A legate differs from a delegate in the strict legal sense. A delegate handles one or many affairs through delegated jurisdiction, often litigation. A legate holds ordinary jurisdiction over an entire country or nation. Because that jurisdiction is ordinary, a legate remains legate even if the appointing pope dies, even if he reaches his post after that death. The pope's right to send legates for unity of faith and discipline was contested since early times. Gregory VII, Paschal II, and John XXII defended it against kings and writers who denied it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lete:
Lete was a Macedonian titular see, known by its coins and inscriptions. The Itinerarium Antonini puts it twenty-five miles from Tupusuctu, or Tiklat, and eighteen miles from Horrea Aninici, now Ain-Roua, south of Bougie. Ancient writers name it: Ptolemy, the younger Pliny, Harpocration, Stephanus Byzantius, and Suidas. In the Middle Ages Nicephorus Bryennius names it too. The spelling Lite is wrong, a product of iotacism. Lete appears in some late Notitiae episcopatuum as suffragan of Thessalonica, later joined to the See of Rentina. The town therefore stood on the Sava, the Oued-Bou-Sellam, but no remains are to be seen.

Greek bishops served Lete and Rentina until the eighteenth century. Lete is now the small village of Aivati, with 1,000 inhabitants, a little north of Salonica.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-da-po:
Lorenzo da Ponte was the poet who wrote Mozart's great opera texts, born at Ceneda in 1749 and dead in New York in 1838. Born Emmanuel Conegliano to a Jewish father, he was baptized with his family in 1763, took the name of his bishop, and trained in the local seminary.

In Vienna he met Mozart and supplied the words for Figaro, Don Giovanni, and Cosi fan tutte. After London and a tangled career, he emigrated to New York, failed in trade and in opera ventures, and settled as a teacher of Italian linked to Columbia College. He also gave America its first lectures on Dante, and lies in an unmarked grave on East Eleventh Street.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorette:
Lorette, full name Notre-Dame de la Jeune Lorette, is a Huron village on the St. Charles River, eight miles north-west of Quebec. In 1908 it held 474 souls, the chief remnant of the ancient Hurons, while related Wyandot lived in Ontario and Oklahoma.

Iroquois raids scattered the Hurons in 1648 and 1649, and missionaries gathered fugitives first on Christian Island, then at Quebec, Orleans Island, and back to Quebec after a Mohawk raid in 1656. Two sub-tribes merged with the Iroquois for peace, but the Cord refused to leave French protection. Their village at Lorette grew from that stubborn remnant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-honore-:
Louis Honore Frechette was a French-Canadian poet, journalist, and politician, born at Levis in 1839 and dead in 1908. After Nicolet seminary he was called to the Quebec bar in 1864, but clients were slow, so he spent seven years in Chicago as a journalist and railroad clerk.

Home in 1871, he won a Commons seat for the Liberals in 1874, lost in 1878 and 1882, and gave up politics for the pen. His poems, from Mes Loisirs in 1863 to La Legende d'un Peuple in 1887 to 1890, won the French Academy's crown in 1879. Prose dramas, letters, and translations followed, and he joined the Royal Society of Canada at its founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-lambill:
Louis Lambillotte was a Belgian Jesuit composer and restorer of Gregorian chant, born near Charleroi in 1796 and dead at Paris in 1855. Organist at fifteen, choirmaster at Saint-Acheul in 1820, he joined the Jesuits in 1825 and taught music across their colleges for thirty years.

He poured out motets, masses, oratorios, and cantiques, French sacred songs, for student choirs and orchestras, and the pieces spread through schools. Late in life he regretted printing hasty improvisations unrevised, and pupils revised them after his death in 1870. His deeper fame lies in chant research, which revived Gregorian music on scientific lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lunette:
A lunette, also called lunula or melchisedech in Germany, is a crescent-shaped clip of gold or silver-gilt. It holds the Host upright when exposed in a monstrance. The crescent sits on a small stand that slots into a groove in the monstrance, fixing it firm.

In use before the Reformation and found in many fifteenth-century monstrances, it was described in detail by Jakob Muller in 1591. He urged that its two strips come apart for cleaning when the Host is changed. Today, as a guard against accidents, the Host more often sits in a glass-faced pyx, itself set into the monstrance, though the rule still bars it from touching the glass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-antoine:
Marie Antoinette was Queen of France, born at Vienna in 1755 and executed at Paris in 1793. She was youngest daughter of Emperor Francis I and Maria Theresa. Her marriage to Louis XVI crowned Choiseul's policy, but she shared from the start the odium of the Franco-Austrian alliance.

In private life she deserves blame for extravagance between 1774 and 1777, with sleigh races, opera balls, hunting, gambling, and Trianon amusements feeding slander. She told Mercy she sought distraction for childlessness, and Prince de Ligne testified her supposed gallantry was only deep friendship and ordinary coquetry. In 1789 crowds hailed her foe Orleans in her hearing, and October mobs drove the court from Versailles to Paris. Her 1791 flight with Fersen and Bouille failed at Varennes. Secret talks with foreign powers could not save the king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-lataste:
Marie Lataste was a French mystic, born at Mimbaste near Dax in 1822 and dead at Rennes in 1847. She was youngest child of simple, pious peasants. By her own account, written under obedience, she was a poor country girl. 

As a troublesome, proud, and self-contained child she taxed her mother's prayers. Her first Communion at twelve turned her life, with a strong sense of God's presence. In 1840 Abbe Pierre Darbins became cure of Mimbaste, and Marie, by what she took as divine command, opened her soul to him. He tested her obedience and humility, found her wholly submissive, and with Dax seminary's director ordered her to write down all she had heard and seen in the supernatural order. She entered the Society of the Sacred Heart in Paris in 1844 and died young at Rennes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquette:
Marquette was a diocese covering Michigan's upper peninsula and nearby islands, under the names Sault Ste Marie and Marquette. Jesuits Raymbault and Jogues first set foot on Michigan soil at Sault Ste Marie in 1641, planting a great cross on the St Marys River. Rene Menard wintered at L'Anse in 1660 to 1661 with little success among resident Indians and later perished in northern Wisconsin.

Claude Allouez passed the Sault in 1665 toward La Pointe, labouring two years before returning to Quebec. After Cadillac failed to hold lower-state Indians with gifts, the government re-manned the fort and asked Jesuits back, with Father Marest first to return. Later missionaries included Badin, Mazzuchelli, Pierz, and Menet, first stationary Jesuit since 1703, plus Jacker, who found Marquette's grave at St Ignace. Bishop Baraga found three churches and two priests and left fifteen priests and twenty-one churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-fernan:
Martin Fernandez Navarrete was a Spanish navigator and writer, born at Avalos in 1765 and dead at Madrid in 1844. Schooled partly at home and partly at Vergara seminary, he joined the navy at fifteen and served with distinction against Gibraltar in 1782. Overwork broke his health, forcing a rest that turned him to historical research.

In 1789 the Marine Minister charged him to search national archives for Spain's maritime history, a three-year task that unearthed Columbus's first and third voyage diaries. He rejoined the navy in 1792, fought at Toulon's siege, and rose to captain. At the Marine Office he planned the hydrographical office, heading it from 1823. In 1808 he quit office rather than accept Joseph Bonaparte, later directing the Academy of History from 1824. His great Coleccion de los viajes of 1825 to 1837, on Spanish sea voyages since the late fifteenth century, made his reputation, besides a fine Cervantes life of 1819.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missionaries-:
Priests who looked after the crowds of pilgrims on the mountain banded together in 1852 at the shrine of Our Lady of La Salette. That band became the Missionaries of La Salette. In 1858 these priests set up a small community with temporary constitutions under the Bishop of Grenoble. Bishop Fava gave them fuller rules in 1876, and Rome gave the institute its approval in May 1890.

Diocesan priests were hard to draw in, so the fathers opened a missionary college, an apostolic school, in 1876. After six years of classical study in the novitiate, students learned above all to fight the great sins the Virgin's words at La Salette had denounced. The congregation spread in time to Belgium, Madagascar, Poland, Brazil, and the United States, and its constitutions won approval in 1909.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mozarabic-rit:
The Mozarabic Rite is the liturgy used generally in Spain and what became Portugal from the earliest known times until the later eleventh century. It still survives in the Capilla Muzarabe of Toledo cathedral and in a chapel of old Salamanca cathedral. Its name is misleading, since it comes from the Mozarabs, Christians living under Moorish rule who kept the rite after Christian Spain abolished it. The rite itself shows no Arab influence.

Also called Gothic, Toledan and Isidorian, it developed under the Visigoths and reached its classic form through Saint Isidore of Seville. The entry treats its history and origin, its manuscripts and editions, the liturgical year, the Divine Office, and the Mass with its distinctive prayers and variable parts. It closes with its occasional services for baptism, marriage and burial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-napoleon-bona:
Napoleon Bonaparte, Emperor of the French, was the second son of Charles Marie Bonaparte and Maria Laetitia Ramolino. He was born at Ajaccio in Corsica on 15 August 1769 and died on Saint Helena on 5 May 1821. His childhood passed in Corsica. Late in 1778 he entered the college of Autun, then the military schools of Brienne in 1779 and Paris in 1783.

His military genius showed in December 1793, at twenty-four, in retaking Toulon from the English. He rose swiftly through the Revolution's wars, commanded in Italy and Egypt, seized power in 1799, and crowned himself emperor in 1804. The entry follows his campaigns, his codes and administration, and his relations with the Church from Concordat to captivity of the pope. It covers his fall, exile to Elba, the Hundred Days, Waterloo, and his last years on Saint Helena.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nazarite:
A Nazarite, Hebrew for consecrated to God, is a person set apart and especially consecrated to the Lord. Though Nazarites appear in early Hebrew history, the Law mentions them specifically only in Numbers 6, a late legal section codifying long-standing usage. Those regulations cover persons consecrating themselves for a set time by temporary vow, but there were also lifelong Nazarites, and children consecrated by parents.

By Numbers 6, Nazarites of either sex must abstain during consecration from wine and all intoxicating drink, and even from all vineyard products in any form. Their hair must grow as a mark of holiness. They may not approach any corpse, even a nearest relative's, on pain of defilement and forfeiture of consecration. If accidentally defiled, they must shave the head of consecration, repeat it on the seventh day, and on the eighth present two turtle doves or young pigeons at the sanctuary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neophyte:
A neophyte, from Greek for the newly planted, is a term for all who have lately entered a new and higher state of life. Newly planted means incorporated with the mystical Body of Christ. It covers beginners in ecclesiastical life or in a religious order. More particularly it means those lately converted from heathenism, transplanted by baptism into the Church's higher life.

From very early times, rules barred neophytes in this last sense from too swift promotion to Holy Orders and positions of responsibility. Nicaea's second canon legislates on the subject, since time is needed for the catechumenate and fuller probation after baptism. The apostolic decree is clear: not a neophyte, lest being puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. The waiting period is not fixed, but left to the bishop's discretion for each case.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-o-deus-ego-am:
O Deus ego amo te, Latin for O God, I love thee, opens two lyrics of uncertain date and authorship, sometimes tied to Francis Xavier. The better known runs five stanzas in matching rhythm, its last three paraphrasing Ignatius of Loyola's prayer of self-offering.

Probably first printed at Cologne in 1695, the hymn gained the title Desire of Saint Ignatius in 1822 and won English versions from Caswall, Keble, and others. A companion lyric with the same opening, the entry notes, follows a different path through hymnals. Zabuesnig’s 1822 hymnal gave the hymn the title Desire of Saint Ignatius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oblates-of-ma:
The Oblates of Mary Immaculate, founded in 1816 as Missionaries of Provence, became a worldwide missionary congregation under Eugène de Mazenod. Born at Aix in 1782 and exiled by the Revolution, Mazenod entered Saint-Sulpice in 1808, was ordained in 1811, and gathered companions at Aix in 1818.

Leo XII approved the congregation in 1826, and Mazenod, later bishop of Marseilles, ruled it until his death in 1861. Priests and lay brothers together preached parish missions, served the poor, and spread from France to Canada, Africa, and Asia, as the entry's later sections detail. Mazenod served as vicar-general of Marseilles in 1823 and bishop there from 1837.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orange-free-s:
The Orange Free State, a province of the Union of South Africa, lies on a high grassy plateau between the Orange and Vaal rivers. Named for the Orange River along its southern edge, it covers 50,392 square miles and held 387,315 people in 1904, only 142,679 of them white.

Dry air and cool nights at four to five thousand feet suited sufferers from lung troubles, while treeless plains turned interesting only near the Drakensberg in the east. Pastoral farming ruled, though fine corn land lay beside Basutoland, and the entry details towns, schools, and churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordinariate:
An ordinariate, a term used chiefly in Germany, names collectively the organs through which an ordinary, especially a bishop, exercises authority. The word does not occur in strict canonical language, where canonists say curia instead, but the two mean the same machinery.

Just as the pope answers for all done in his name through the Roman Curia's congregations, tribunals, and offices. So a bishop answers for his vicar-general, officials, judges, secretaries, and councils, whose acts compose his diocesan administration. The term is used particularly in Germany, not in strict canonical language.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paraclete:
Paraclete, or Comforter, is a title of the Holy Spirit, from the Greek parakletos. As a name for the Spirit it occurs only in Saint John's Gospel, at 14:16 and 26, 15:26, and 16:7, and has been rendered advocate, intercessor, teacher, helper, and comforter. Comforter, though at odds with the Greek passive form, is backed by Hellenistic usage, old versions, Fathers, liturgy, and John's own context.

John's mission for the Paraclete is to dwell with disciples after Jesus withdraws His visible presence. He brings home inwardly the teaching Christ gave outwardly, and witnesses to the Saviour's doctrine and work. That comfort is not fenced to apostles alone, as Gospel promises and Acts 2 show. Cardinal Manning sees here a new dispensation, that of the Spirit as Sanctifier, guarding the Church's truth and fostering her holiness and each soul's life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patriarch-and:
Patriarch and patriarchate name the highest church dignitaries after the pope, and the lands they rule. Patriarch comes from Greek for father or chief of a race. It appears in the Septuagint for tribal chiefs. In the New Testament it marks Abraham as father of many nations, David, and Jacob's twelve sons. That last use fixed the word for Scripture figures, while litany calls still invoke all holy patriarchs and prophets.

Early church titles borrowed from civil life or Jewish usage, and patriarch belongs to the Jewish class, given to bishops of special dignity by analogy with Old Law fathers. At first the name was loose honour without strict sense, though the reality came before the title. Later pages trace the five great patriarchates, Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem, their rights, rivalries, and the title's spread to lesser sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-du-c:
Philippe du Contant de La Molette was a French theologian and biblical scholar, born at Côte-Saint-André in Dauphiné in 1737. He studied at the Sorbonne. In 1765 he defended a thesis on Job in six languages, pleasing Louis XV so much that the king waived the delays for his licentiate examinations. He never used the privilege. He later became vicar-general of Vienne.

As a biblical author he showed wide erudition and command of Oriental tongues, but little originality, and his criticism often misleads. His Paris works explain Genesis against Voltaire, Exodus, the Psalms, and Leviticus from primitive texts, with essays on Scripture, Hebrew poetry, and music. He also prepared a new polyglot Bible, though whether it ever appeared is doubtful. He died on the scaffold during the Terror in 1793.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontius-pilat:
Pontius Pilate was the Roman procurator of Judea whose long rule, from A.D. 26 to 36, covers the whole public ministry of John the Baptist and of Jesus. Fifth in succession after Valerius Gratus, he held more than the usual financial powers, with supreme judicial authority as well. He owed his post to the influence of Sejanus.

His name bears lasting infamy for his part in the Crucifixion, though he would gladly have acquitted Christ and tried hard to do so. He yielded when his own position was threatened, a portrait the entry draws of a worldly man who knows the right yet gives way under pressure. Philo calls him inflexible, merciless, and obstinate, and the Jews hated his severity and his disregard for their customs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prelate:
A real prelate holds a prelature, a church office with special and stable jurisdiction and precedence. An honorary prelate holds the marks of the dignity with no matching office. The first prelates are the bishops, holding jurisdiction over the Church's members by Divine institution. Apart from bishops, real prelates include those with quasi episcopal, free jurisdiction over a land cut from a diocese. Such is the prelate nullius, as with Monte Cassino, Einsiedeln, and St Maurice in Wallis.

They also include diocesan officers with free and proper jurisdiction, such as earlier archdeacons and cathedral provosts and deans. They include abbots and provosts of monasteries, who hold but the lasting mark of the house. They include titular bishops, both those who hold supreme rule in vicariates apostolic and other lands, and those who hold but episcopal consecration with no rule over a district.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-primate:
In the Western Church a primate, from Latin primas, from primus, first, is a bishop with superior authority. It reaches beyond his own province's bishops, past the metropolitan's scope, over several provinces and metropolitans. This touches church jurisdiction and organization, not episcopal powers, which each bishop holds in full.  The post has no uniform shape and no common-law place: primatial rights count as privileges.

At widest, those rights would cover calling and heading national councils, crowning the sovereign, hearing appeals from metropolitan and even episcopal courts, and lastly the honorary right of precedence. The frame, once useful in binding national churches, has lost weight and faded, first since national churches as such are no more. Second, the slow disciplinary pull of the Western churches toward Rome drew power to the centre. Save for Gran in Hungary, the primatial title is now but honorary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-proselyte:
Proselyte is the English word for a convert to Judaism. It appears only in the New Testament. This short encyclopedia entry traces the Greek word proselytos, meaning stranger or newcomer. By 300 BC it carried a local and political sense. In New Testament times it gained a technical religious sense. In the Septuagint the same word often means a foreigner living in Palestine.

Two groups come into view. Strict proselytes accepted circumcision and kept the Jewish Law in full. Beside them stood the God-fearers of Acts. These were sympathetic friends of the synagogue, drawn by Jewish monotheism and moral ideals. They did not become full converts. Saint Paul preached to these God-fearers on his journeys. From them he gathered the first members of many of his churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-revision-of-v:
The revision of the Vulgate began in spring 1907, when the press announced that Pius the Tenth would prepare a critical revision of the Latin Bible. The need had long been recognized, and it stood in the Biblical Commission's programme, founded by Leo the Thirteenth. Despite forty years of care over Clement the Eighth's authentic edition of 1592, its text was known from the first to need revision. In some ways it stood below the Sixtine version of 1590 it had hastily replaced.

Recent decades, pre-eminently an age of critical textual study, had pressed the case anew. The Commission spent two years gathering every printed Biblical text into its Rome working-room, a difficult and costly collection already proving its use, and began collating manuscript variants. The pope met the first printing costs, and the faithful's generosity, above all in America, has kept the work going since.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhenish-palat:
The Rhenish Palatinate was a former German electorate, named for the palsgrave, or count palatine, a royal official of the old Empire. In Carolingian times the count palatine was merely the king's representative in the high court of justice. Otto the Great appointed one for Bavaria in 937, to supervise crown lands and imperial revenues and check the duke's power. The palsgrave of Lorraine at Aachen later ranked foremost.

In 1155, after Hermann of Stableck's death, Frederick Barbarossa gave the countship to his half-brother Conrad, who joined its lands to his own. The later story runs through the Reformation princes. Frederick the Fourth led German Protestantism and founded the Evangelical Union in 1608. Frederick the Fifth, whose acceptance of Bohemia's crown helped unleash the Thirty Years' War, lost his Winter Kingdom and his electorate after defeat at Weissen Berg near Prague in 1620.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-grosse:
Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, ranked among the Middle Ages' most learned men. Born about 1175 to a poor family at Stradbroke in Suffolk, he reached Oxford no later than 1192 or 1193. By 1199 Giraldus Cambrensis was commending him to the Bishop of Hereford for his grasp of the liberal arts, literature, law, and medicine, and for his character and industry. Study and teaching of theology at Paris are probable, though not certain.

Back at Oxford early in the thirteenth century, he became head of the university and held four archdeaconries in turn. An illness in 1232, joined to deepened religious feeling and love of poverty, moved him to resign all preferments save the Lincoln prebend. Freely elected Bishop of Lincoln in 1235, he was consecrated at Reading the next year. The entry treats his many activities separately, from teaching and philosophy to his French religious romance, the Chasteau d'Amour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-white:
Robert White was an English composer of the Elizabethan age, ranked among the finest of his generation despite long neglect. Born about 1530 and trained by his father, he took his music doctorate at Cambridge in 1560. In 1561 he took over from Dr Tye as Ely's organist and master of the choristers, serving until 1566. He then held the same post at Chester.

His repute as choir trainer won him the organist's post at Westminster Abbey in 1570. Though a Catholic, he kept that post until his death in November 1574, one of three Catholics directing the music of the Chapel Royal, the Abbey, and St Paul's. Many compositions survive, and his Latin motets place him in the front rank. His Lamentations for five voices and motets such as Peccatum peccavit Jerusalem show a flavour ahead of his time. Burney later unearthed his neglected works, and modern scholars rank him with Tallis and Byrd.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruthenian-rit:
There is, properly speaking, no separate Ruthenian rite. The name is used for Ruthenian modifications of the Byzantine or Greek Rite. These came about in two ways. First, ancient Slavonic missals in Russia and Little Russia differed from Greek use at Constantinople. When Ruthenians united with the Holy See in 1595, they brought several usages Nikon later corrected at Moscow. Where differences denied no faith, the Holy See let them stand.

Second, after union became fixed, Polish Latin clergy and laity saw apparent contradictions of faith in Greek ceremonies. The Greek Ruthenian clergy at the Synod of Zamosc in 1720 changed the Byzantine Rite, particularly the Mass, to express unity with Roman brethren. Russian authors bitterly call these changes latinizing, and most were probably unnecessary. Chief modifications were adding the Filioque to the Creed and commemorating the Pope of Rome in the Ektene and Great Entrance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-peter-o:
Peter of Sebaste, youngest child of Basil and Emmelia of Caesarea, was born about 340 and died in 391. His family produced Macrina the Younger and the great Cappadocian teachers Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, and his eldest sister Macrina shaped his religious training. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a quiet brother in a famous household.

Giving up secular learning for Scripture and the ascetic life, Peter was ordained priest by his brother Basil, then withdrew to solitude. He helped Macrina and his mother build their monastic community after his father's death, and around 380 he became bishop of Sebaste. The entry leans on Gregory's Life of Macrina, and shows a bishop formed less by public debate than by family holiness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samar-and-ley:
Samar and Leyte are two civil provinces in the Visayan islands of the Philippines, together forming the diocese of Calbayog, suffragan of Manila. The provinces take in Sámar, 5,031 square miles, Leyte, 2,722, and smaller islands from Balicuatro to Panaon. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes a young diocese at the edge of the archipelago.

Jesuit missionaries reached Leyte and Samar in 1595, and the islands belonged to Cebú until they became a separate diocese on 10 April 1910. Pablo Singzon de la Anunciacion, formerly vicar-general of Cebú, became first bishop, consecrated at St Francis's in Manila that June. Lazarist Fathers ran the seminary and college of St Vincent de Paul at Calbayog, seat of the diocese, a city of 22,000 on Samar's western side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sarum-rite:
The Sarum Rite, more exactly Sarum Use, is the way of ordering the Roman liturgy that ruled pre-Reformation southern England and spread across much of Scotland and Ireland. York, Lincoln, Bangor, and Hereford had their own, not very different, uses in the north and Wales. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a liturgy from Rome to Salisbury.

Anglo-Saxon Christians knew no liturgy but Rome's. The synod of Clovesho in 747 ordered one manner for feasts, baptism, Mass, and chant. It followed the pattern received in writing from the Roman Church, with the seven canonical hours kept everywhere in fitting psalmody. From that common root, Salisbury's books grew into the Use that shaped English worship until the Reformation, and the entry maps its missal, breviary, and customs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schenute:
Schenute, also called Schenudi or Sinuthius, was a Coptic abbot. His birth is dated to 332, 333, or 334, and his death to 451, 452, or 466, all accounts agreeing he lived about 118 years. Born at Schenalolet near Akhmim, he died in his own monastery, still standing as Deir-el-Abiad, the White Monastery, near Atripe. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia honours the father of the Coptic Church.

He became a monk in 371 at the great double monastery ruled by his uncle Bgol, whom he succeeded as abbot in 388. Cyril of Alexandria, whom he accompanied to Ephesus in 431, named him archimandrite during that council. Under Bgol and Schenute, Pachomius's rule grew stricter, above all through the introduction of vows, each monk solemnly professing in church to keep the monastery's rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebaste:
Sebaste, a titular see in Phrygia Pacatiana suffragan of Laodicea, is known apart from Hierocles's list by its coins and still more by its inscriptions. Those inscriptions fix it as modern Sivasli, in fertile country at the foot of Bourgas Dagh in the eastern Banaz plain. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia reconstructs a town from stones.

Augustus founded Sebaste and settled villagers from nearby places there. The Phrygian god Men with his Greek counterpart Zeus, plus Apollo and Artemis, were worshipped in the town. Strategi or archons ran it, with a council, or gerousia, set up in 99. Several inscriptions are Christian. Le Quien names seven bishops, six known from council signatures, among them Modestus at Chalcedon in 451 and Anatolius at Constantinople in 553.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-andrew-of-:
St. Andrew of Crete, theologian, homilist, and hymnographer, was born at Damascus about the middle of the seventh century. He died on 4 July 740, or 720, the day his feast is kept in the Greek Church. This entry follows a boy who at fifteen went to Jerusalem, entered a monastery, joined the clerics of Theodore, Bishop of Jerusalem. He rose until Theodore sent him in 685 to congratulate Emperor Constantine Pogonatus on the Sixth General Council.

Remaining at Constantinople, he was ordained deacon, distinguished himself again, and was appointed metropolitan of Gortyna in Crete. At first an opponent of the Monothelite heresy, he attended the conciliabulum of 712 that undid the council's decrees, but amended his error the next year. The entry presents a hymn writer whose lapses never dimmed his fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-colette:
St. Colette, diminutive of Nicoletta or Coletta, founded the Colettine Poor Clares. She was born 13 January 1381 at Corbie in Picardy, France. She died at Ghent on 6 March 1447. This entry follows a girl whose father, Robert Boellet, was carpenter of the famous Corbie Benedictine Abbey, and whose mother was Marguerite Moyon. Colette joined successively the Beguines, the Benedictines, and the Urbanist Poor Clares, then lived as a recluse for a while.

Resolved on reforming the Poor Clares, she approached the antipope Benedict XIII, Pedro de Luna, whom France then recognized as rightful pope. Benedict allowed her to enter the order of Poor Clares. His Bulls of 1406, 1407, 1408, and 1412 empowered her to found new convents and finish the order's reform. The Countess of Geneva approved, as did Henri de la Beaume, her Franciscan confessor and spiritual guide. Colette began her work at Beaume, in the Geneva diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-boste:
John Boste, priest and martyr of Durham, stayed resolute, bold, joyful, and pleasant even on the rack. Raised by a good Catholic family of Dufton in Westmoreland about 1544, he studied at Queen's College, Oxford, from 1569 to 1572. He won a fellowship, then entered the Church at Brome in Suffolk during 1576. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Durham to 24 July 1594.

He gave up his fellowship in 1580 and went to Reims, was ordained priest on 4 March 1581, and reached England that April, landing at Hartlepool. As a zealous missioner he drew extraordinary efforts from persecutors. Betrayed by Eglesfield at William Claxton's house at Waterhouses near Durham on 5 July 1593, he was carried to London and terribly racked in the Tower. Returned to Durham for the July assizes of 1594, he faced death with undaunted courage, steadying a fellow martyr who had recanted through fear.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-mallo:
Stephen Mallory White, an American statesman, forced Pacific railroads to repay the government and urged the Panama Canal. Born at San Francisco on 19 January 1853 to William F. White and Fannie Russell, natives of Limerick and distinguished California pioneers of 1849, he was grand-nephew of the poet Gerald Griffin and cousin of Confederate navy secretary Stephen Russell Mallory.

Schooled at the Jesuit colleges of St Ignatius in San Francisco and Santa Clara, he was admitted to the bar in 1874. A noted orator and profound student, he worked with tireless energy as lawyer and public servant. Elected as a Democrat state senator in 1886, lieutenant governor in 1888, and United States senator in 1893, he served six years. In the Senate he led the fight making railroads pay their enormous debt and pressed canal construction. He died at Los Angeles on 21 February 1901.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-white:
Stephen White of Clonmel was born in 1574. He was an Irish Jesuit scholar, counted among the most learned men of his age. This entry follows him from Trinity College, Dublin, which he left rather than swear the oath of supremacy, to Salamanca, where he joined the Society of Jesus in 1596.

From Spain he moved on to teach theology in German towns. His great love was Irish history. He helped shape a language method later used by Comenius, fixed the name Scotia to Ireland, and sent corrected Irish manuscripts to scholars like Ussher and Colgan. His Apologia pro Hibernia answered Camden's attacks on Ireland. He died at Galway in 1646.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-symmachus-the:
Symmachus the Ebionite wrote a Greek version of the Old Testament that Origen included in his Hexapla and Tetrapla. Fragments survive in what remains of the Hexapla, while his Commentaries, apparently written to back Ebionite teaching by attacking Matthew's Gospel, are lost. Origen says he got them from a woman named Juliana, who had inherited them from Symmachus himself.

Palladius preserves Origen's note of finding the book in Juliana's house at Caesarea while in hiding there, probably in 238 to 241. Epiphanius placed Symmachus under Severus, but his text is full of blunders, and a Syriac translator reads Verus, meaning Marcus Aurelius. Other ancient writers agree unanimously that Symmachus was an Ebionite, not a Samaritan convert.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taubate:
Taubaté is a Brazilian diocese, established 29 April 1908 as suffragan of São Paulo. Its first bishop, Epaminondas Nuñes de Avila e Silva, born in 1869 and consecrated in 1909, took up his duties on 21 November 1909. The town holds a cathedral counted among Brazil's finest, plus churches of Sant' Anna, Nossa Senhora do Pilar, and Santa Clara, built in 1644. Chapels serve the San José school, Santa Isabel Hospital, and the Mendicant Asylum.

Catholic schools include the Seminario Menor under Capuchins, two colleges under Sisters of St Joseph, and two more under the Third Order of St Francis. Orders in the diocese are Capuchins, Franciscans, and Sisters of St Joseph. Seven religious brotherhoods exist, and the diocesan paper O Labaro was founded by the bishop. Sources point readers to the article on Brazil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thagaste:
Thagaste, or Tagaste, was a titular see in Numidia and a rather important municipality. Pliny and the Antonine Itinerary mention it, but its history is unknown. It is famous as St Augustine's birthplace, born there in 354 to Patricius and St Monica. Augustine speaks of a Thagaste monastery where he lived with Severus, later Bishop of Milevis. Only three bishops are known: St Firmus of the late third century, St Alypius, and Januarius, exiled by Huneric in 484.

The see still existed about 600. At the French occupation the land belonged to the Arabized Berber Hanensha, bordering Tunisia. Thagaste is now Souk Ahras, capital of a commune of 7,500, in a mixed community of 42,600, in Constantine department, Algeria. The modern town stands on a small peaked plateau, well served by railways, and thrives on vineyards, cattle, forests, and mining. Ruins of a basilica and Christian monuments have been found.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-absolute:
The Absolute is a term of philosophy, applied to the Supreme Being. It signifies first that which is complete, second that which exists by its own nature and is independent of everything else, and third that which is related to no other being. Fourth, it is the sum of all being, actual, in Hegel's sense. In the first two senses Christian philosophy may accept it as a name for God.

Though the term was not current in the Middle Ages, Scholastics used equivalents. They spoke of God as Pure Actuality, as uncaused Being, or as containing every perfection. St Thomas stresses God's absoluteness, showing He falls under no genus or species and His essence is His existence. Aquinas faced the difficulty that the unrelated Absolute cannot be First Cause, since causation implies relation. His solution holds God and creatures related, but the relation is real in effects, conceptual in God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-celtic-ri:
Worship in early Britain, Ireland, Brittany, and the Irish missions abroad is gathered here under the Celtic Rite, a term the entry warns against reading as one uniform system. Seven heads organise the survey, later eight in the text: history and origin, manuscript sources, Divine Office, Mass, baptism, care of the sick, consecration of churches, and hymns.

Evidence survives in scraps, and much written on the subject rests on conjecture shaped by controversy. Diversity, not sameness, marks the rites of Columbanus's monasteries in France, Germany, Switzerland, and Italy. Manuscripts such as the Stowe Missal and the Bangor Antiphonary anchor the discussion, giving readers a sober guide to a fragmentary field.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-gallican-:
Worship in Gaul before Rome's rite prevailed is reconstructed here across six heads: history, manuscripts, liturgical year, Divine Office, Mass, and occasional services. From the earliest records until about the middle or end of the eighth century, the Gallican Rite shaped prayer in France. Evidence before the fifth century is absent, and scant even then.

Diversity, not uniformity, marks the rite, though its broad pattern holds together. Spain's Mozarabic Rite stood so close that scholars often speak of a Hispano-Gallican family, with chapels at Toledo and Salamanca preserving it as a living relic. Manuscripts and descriptions let readers glimpse a liturgy Charlemagne's reforms displaced.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-rite-of-c:
Worship of Constantinople, second only to Rome in worldwide spread, is laid out here under its Byzantine name. Its liturgies, Office, sacraments, blessings, and exorcisms reach over a hundred million Christians. They include all Orthodox Churches, Melkites in Syria and Egypt, Uniats in the Balkans, and Italo-Greeks in Calabria, Apulia, Sicily, and Corsica. 

Not an original parent rite, it derives from Antioch, following that liturgy's disposition of parts. Alexandria places the great intercession before consecration; Antioch, and therefore Constantinople, orders it differently. History, the Liturgy of Saint James's yearly use at Jerusalem, and the rite's structure guide readers through Eastern worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-roman-rit:
Rome's manner of worship, the most widespread in Christendom, is defined here in one compact entry. It covers celebration of the Holy Sacrifice, administration of sacraments, recitation of the Divine Office, and other functions such as blessings and sacramentals, as used in the city and diocese of Rome. Archaic antiquity, dignity, beauty, and comparative brevity mark it.

Spread came not from those advantages but from Rome's exalted see. Local bishops, kings, and emperors adopted the rite of the chief bishop of all, feeling they could do no better. Imitation carried the Eastern principle westward: rite follows patriarchate. History and present use close a crisp guide to Latin worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-vatican-a:
Rome's busiest scientific workshop, judged by output, is the Vatican as this entry presents it. Materials of the highest order lie stored in the palace in astonishing abundance, open to easy access under favourable working conditions. Apart from the newest theories, for which Vatican treasures offer nothing, every branch of human knowledge finds sources there.

Philosophy, theology, history, literature, philology, jurisprudence, geography, ethnology, and art all suffer, the entry complains, from great and partly absolute neglect as histories of science. Despite the Curia's strained finances, the pope yearly raised appropriations for science within the palace. Libraries, archives, and observatory work follow in a celebration of learning behind Vatican walls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-young-men:
California's Catholic fraternal order, grown national, is the subject here, founded on 4 March 1883 at San Francisco. Six founders launched it. John McDade served as first grand president and later first supreme president, James Smith later joined Washington's Commerce Court, and Edward Sheehan, William Ryan, William Gagan, and George Maxwell completed the group. Preliminary meetings and long deliberation produced a constitution, adopted with officers elected. 

Only beneficial and fraternal organisation born in the West to turn national, it pledges mutual aid and benevolence. It also seeks moral, social, and intellectual improvement, and devotion to Church and loyalty to country, under the motto Pro Deo, Pro Patria. Supreme Council holds legislative and appellate power over councils spreading across the nation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thelepte:
Byzacene's titular see Thelepte, a Roman colony at a road junction, is the small city described here. Roads branch north to Cilium and Theveste, south to Gafsa and Gabes. In the sixth century it housed Byzacene's military governor, and Procopius records Justinian's fortification of the city. Bishops' names survive across centuries of councils and exiles. 

Julian attended Carthage in 256, and Donatianus the Conference of Carthage in 411, perhaps a council at home in 418. Frumentius suffered exile under Huneric in 484, and Stephen sat at Byzacene's council in 641. Native son Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe, adds lustre. Ruins at Medinet el-Kedima near Gafsa, with a Byzantine citadel in utter ruin, mark the site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theveste:
Numidian city Theveste, now Tebessa in Algeria, is the Roman town traced here as a titular see. Important even before Christianity, it housed Legio III Augusta in the first century ere the legion moved to Lambaesis. Trajan likely made it a colonia, and Donatists held a council there. Saints Lucius, Maximilianus, and Crispina shed blood for the faith in its early years.

Lucius, its bishop, sat at Carthage in 256 and died for the faith two years later. Maximilianus fell on 12 March 295, Crispina on 5 December 304. Later bishops Romulus in 349, Urbicus in 411, Felix exiled by Vandals in 484, and Palladius in an inscription mark its line. Patrician Solomon rebuilt it under Justinian and raised a tomb there that still stands. French rule from 1851 made Tebessa a canton capital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-conect:
Thomas Conecte, a Carmelite reformer born at Rennes late in the fourteenth century, won fame as a fiery preacher before dying at Rome in 1433. His sermons at Cambrai, Tournai and Arras attacked fashionable women's headgear so sharply that hearers stripped off their ornaments on the spot, while gamblers burned their cards and dice. His attacks on lax priests forced him to flee for safety.

He then turned to reforming his own order, setting up a strict observance near Florence that grew into the Congregation of Mantua. Visiting that house in 1432, he went on to Venice and Rome, where his fierce words against the Curia brought a charge of conspiracy. Condemned as a heretic, he was publicly burned, a sentence Pope Eugene IV is said to have regretted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-white:
Thomas White, also known as Blacklow, was a theologian born in Essex in 1593 whose forty books stirred a bitter controversy, dying in London in 1676. Grandson of the lawyer Edmund Plowden, he was educated at St. Omer, Valladolid and Douai, ordained priest in 1617, and taught theology at Douai until 1630, when he became president of the English College at Lisbon.

Resigning in 1633, he returned to England and wrote on purgatory, hell, papal infallibility and passive obedience to any established government, in language critics called new and unscholastic. The Inquisition censured several opinions in 1655 and 1657, and friends and former students publicly disowned his principles. In the end he gave up the censured opinions and placed himself and his writings under the Holy See's judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ugolino-brunf:
Ugolino Brunforte, often called Ugolino of Monte Giorgio, was a Franciscan chronicler born about 1262. He died about 1348. His father Rinaldo, lord of Sarnano in the Marches, came of an old noble French house, kin to Countess Matilda. Ugolino joined the Friars Minor at sixteen, spent his novitiate at Roccabruna, and lived mostly at Santa Maria in Monte Giorgio. Chosen Bishop of Teramo in 1295, he lost the post when Celestine V resigned before his consecration and Boniface VIII annulled the appointment.

Nearly fifty years later he was elected provincial of Macerata, a late honour in a quiet career. Scholars now credit Ugolino with the Fioretti, the beloved little flowers of St Francis. That book gathers tales about the saint and his first companions. The entry weighs the evidence for that credit and lists his other writings, giving the life behind one of the most charming books of the Franciscan tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-eustace-w:
Eustace White was a martyr born at Louth in Lincolnshire in 1560, who suffered at London's Tyburn on 10 December 1591. His parents were heretics, and his conversion drew his father's curse. After schooling at Reims in 1584 and Rome in 1586, where ordination followed, he reached the mission in November 1588 and worked in England's west.

On 1 September 1591 he was betrayed at Blandford in Dorset by a lawyer with whom he had debated religion. Across two days he debated a minister in public and greatly impressed the Protestants watching. Sent to London and lodged in Bridewell on 18 September, he lay on straw for forty-six days with hands closely manacled. Examined under torture seven times, hanging by his manacled hands, he stayed firm and suffered at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-nicholas-:
Nicholas Postgate was an English martyr born at Kirkdale House, Egton, Yorkshire, in 1596 or 1597, who died at York on 7 August 1679. He entered Douai College on 11 July 1621 and took the college oath on 12 March 1623. He received minor orders on 23 December 1624, the diaconate on 18 March 1628, and the priesthood two days later. He was sent on the mission on 29 June 1630.

He laboured in his native country with great benefit to hundreds of souls, and Thomas Ward, who later wrote of him, knew him well. The exciseman Reeves seized him at Matthew Lyth's house at Sleights, Little Beck, near Whitby, and he was condemned under 27 Elizabeth, chapter 2, for being a priest. His quarters were given to friends for burial, one hand was sent to Douai, and his portable altar stone is still venerated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-richard-w:
Richard White, truly Gwyn, was a martyr born at Llanidloes in Montgomeryshire about 1537, executed at Wrexham in Denbighshire on 15 October 1584. After a brief stay at Oxford he read at St John's College, Cambridge, until about 1562. He then became a schoolmaster, first at Overton in Flintshire, then at Wrexham and elsewhere, winning considerable repute as a Welsh scholar. Six children were born to him and his wife Catherine, three of whom survived him.

For a while he conformed in religion, but he was reconciled to the Catholic Church when the seminary priests first reached Wales. For his recusancy he was arrested more than once, and in 1579 he lay in Ruthin jail, offered liberty if he would conform. In 1580 he was moved to Wrexham, where he suffered much persecution, being carried by force to Protestant service, before his trial and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-lui:
Luis de Lapuente, also called de Ponte or Dupont, was a Spanish Jesuit spiritual writer who died at Valladolid in 1624. Born there in 1554, he studied under the celebrated Francisco Suárez, taught philosophy at Salamanca. Showed such talent for governing and forming young religious that ill health alone forced him from offices he had filled with distinction.

His later years were given to writing, and though not counted among Spain's literary classics, his practical spirituality placed him among the great masters of asceticism, the disciplined pursuit of holiness. Ordained in 1580, he directed the mystic Marina de Escobar until his death and nursed plague victims at Villagarcia in 1599. Best known is his Meditations on the Mysteries of Our Holy Faith, translated into ten languages, including Arabic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-west-syrian-r:
The West Syrian Rite is the liturgy used by Syria's Jacobites and Catholic Syrians, in origin simply Antioch's old rite in the Syriac language. The oldest known Antiochene form is Greek, and the many Greek terms remaining in Syriac show derivation from Greek. Made very early, evidently before the Monophysite schism and before Constantinople's Byzantine infiltrations began.

As soon as Christian communities arose in Syria's countryside, prayers said in Greek at Antioch and Jerusalem were naturally translated into the peasants' Syriac. As Silvia's Pilgrimage describes at Jerusalem, lessons first read in Greek then rendered into Syriac for the people. Later sections list the rite's many anaphoras, of St Peter, St John, the Twelve Apostles, St Mark. St Clement, St Dionysius, St Ignatius, St Cyril, Severus of Antioch, James Baradaeus, and a host of others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-flete:
William Flete was an English Augustinian hermit and mystic, close friend of Saint Catherine of Siena. His birthplace and dates are unknown, and his death date is disputed. Schooled at Cambridge, he joined the Austin Friars in England, then sought stricter discipline at two reformed houses near Siena. Reaching the forest of Lecceto, with its caves suited to prayer, he joined that community with his superiors' consent. He studied and prayed in a cave by day and slept in the house at night.

As the Bachelor of the Wood, he heard Catherine's confessions at Lecceto. He loved solitude too much to heed Urban VI's call to Rome during the papal schism. His long praise of Catherine at her death survives with another work at Siena.
