After nineteen austere years in the wood, he may have died in England in 1383, though Lecceto's death book never names him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-wa:
William of Wayneflete was Bishop of Winchester, Chancellor of England, and founder of Magdalen College, Oxford. Born toward the end of the fourteenth century to Richard Patten of Wayneflete, he died at South Waltham on 11 August 1486. Schooled at Winchester College and Oxford, where he graduated in divinity, he took orders by 1426 and mastered Winchester School in 1429. In 1438 he gained Saint Mary Magdalen's hospital mastership, doubling his income.

Henry VI met him at Winchester in 1440 and chose him first master, then in 1443 provost, of the new Eton College. On Beaufort's death in 1447 the king named him Bishop of Winchester, consecrated that July at Eton. Within a year he won a charter for Magdalen Hall at Oxford, replaced a decade later by Magdalen College, endowed richly with lands and a great library. As a peacemaker he calmed Jack Cade's rising in 1450 and laboured for peace against Yorkist plots.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zante:
Zante is the Greek diocese, sole suffragan of Corfu's archdiocese, permanently joined to Cephalonia. It covers Cephalonia, Zante, Ithaca, Santa Maura or Leucas, and Cerigo or Cythera, where among 170,000 people barely 1200 Latin-rite Catholics live. The diocese holds two secular priests, four Capuchin fathers, one brother, three main stations and one auxiliary station, and seven churches and chapels. As early as the fourth century Zante held a Catholic bishop, whose successors fell to the Greek schism.

About 1200 a Latin diocese rose again at Zante, and in 1222 it joined Cephalonia, also fourth-century in origin and later schismatic. In 1386 both became Corfu suffragans. After the Ionian Islands joined Greece in 1863, schismatics oppressed Catholics sorely. Today the diocese has no bishop of its own, the Archbishop of Corfu administers it, and it shows no growth in strength.
celebrated-crimes-complete:
Alexandre Dumas published his Crimes Celebres in Paris in 1839 and 1840, in eight volumes and eighteen titles; this edition gathers the whole set. The introduction in this text calls them source books for the historical novels that followed. Each piece retells a documented crime or scandal in Dumas's full narrative manner.

The Borgias and the Cenci open the series, followed by the Massacres of the South and Mary Stuart. Karl-Ludwig Sand, Urbain Grandier, Derues, and the Marquise de Brinvilliers carry the poisonings, possessions, and assassinations. An essay takes up the Man in the Iron Mask, and Martin Guerre argues the impostor case. The publisher's note warns that facts sometimes bend under the storytelling, and mature readers are expected to allow for it.
celt-and-saxon-complete:
George Meredith's Celt and Saxon, complete in nineteen chapters, is his unfinished novel of Ireland and England. Patrick O'Donnell, a young Irishman of feeling and music, visits Earlsfont, the Adister estate. The Saxon Adisters, proud and reserved, measure him with suspicion. Caroline Adister draws his heart from the first evening.

Dinner parties, a princess's visit, and the Mattock family widen the social picture. Captain Con, Patrick's transparent elder brother, writes a letter that stirs the plot. Mars convalescent, a wounded soldier recovering, ends the fragment. Meredith left the tale unfinished, and it breaks off rather than concludes. What survives is a study of national temperaments, Celt against Saxon, told with unusual sympathy for the Irish side of the argument.
chamisso-peter-schlemihls-wundersame-ges:
Chamisso published the strange story of Peter Schlemihl in 1814, and this volume gives the tale in his original German: Peter Schlemihls wundersame Geschichte. A bottomless purse buys the hero everything except a place among his fellow men. The missing shadow marks him everywhere he goes.

In the author's own language, the story's melancholy music sounds at full strength. German readers have treated the novella as a classic since its first appearance, passing it between generations. Its blend of fairy tale, satire, and quiet despair resists every label. The man who lost himself by degrees becomes a mirror for any reader who has traded too much. Few short books cast so long a shadow.
cleopatra-complete:
Cleopatra in its complete form gathers the whole Alexandria novel by Georg Ebers into one long text, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers, who knew ancient Egypt as a scholar, retells the famous love of Mark Antony and Queen Cleopatra. Around them he builds a second story about Barine, a young Alexandrian woman, and Dion, the man she loves.

Twenty-five chapters carry the action from court parties and building works to secret flights, guarded rooms, and the final Roman victory. The queen's jealousy puts Barine in danger, while Caesarion's desire adds another threat. Private love keeps colliding with state power. Readers who want the full arc in one place, from first meeting to the queen's last defiance, get it here without pausing between volumes.
clotelle-or-the-colored-heroine-a-tale-o:
William Wells Brown wrote Clotelle, in its first form in 1853 and reshaped for this 1867 version, making him the first African American novelist. Brown had escaped slavery himself. His tale grows out of the famous story of an enslaved daughter of a president, sold at auction in New Orleans. It follows its heroine through sale, separation, love, and bold escapes across the slave South.

Brown mixes romance with hard fact: slave markets, families torn apart, and women passing as men or as white to win freedom. Later scenes reach the Civil War, when Black men at last could fight for their own freedom. The novel's shifting versions show Brown rewriting his protest for changing times.
coniston-complete:
Winston Churchill's Coniston stands complete in one file, all four books of the novel. Churchill, the American novelist and no relation to the British statesman, framed the tale with James Russell Lowell's warning on democracy. Boss rule in a small state supplies the public plot. A girl's life supplies the heart that readers remember.

Jethro Bass, a tanner turned political boss, runs legislators through lieutenants, debts, and railroad favors. Cynthia Ware, later Wetherell, grows up in his shadow after her parents' sad early story closes. Orphaned, she is raised by Jethro in the tannery house and taught by the parson. Boston schooling and love for Bob Worthington, heir to opposing interests, test her loyalty. Churchill blends dialect, scenery, and legislative scheming across decades of history. Readers who want the arc, from Jackson's era to the railroad fights, without hunting separate volumes, take the novel in this form.
conscience-complete:
Hector Malot's novel of a murderer's conscience is presented whole in Conscience, Complete, the full English text. Saniel, a poor medical student from Auvergne, begs three thousand francs from his rich comrade Glady and chokes on the humiliation. The moneylender Caffie holds the debt that can end his career before it starts. Saniel reasons his way to murder with a philosopher's calm.

Inside, the killing is planned like a diagnosis, down to a knife chosen to mislead the police. Saniel rises as a Paris doctor while the crime fades from every memory but his own. A second death drags Caffie back into his dreams and ruins his sleep. Phillis and her accused brother then force the choice his conscience has waited years to demand. Readers taking the novel whole get Malot's study of guilt as a slow disease, diagnosed by the doctor who cannot cure himself.
cosmopolis-complete:
Paul Bourget's Cosmopolis stands whole in this complete English edition, a novel of Rome's international society in the 1890s. Bourget studies souls the way doctors study cases. French, Italian, Russian, and American figures meet in Roman salons. Faith, free thought, and fashionable despair collide in their talk and their loves.

Marquis de Montfanon, an aging French Catholic legitimist, anchors the believing side of the argument. He collects papers on the French nobility while dueling in words with a socialist bookseller. Younger visitors chase love, art, and sensation through palaces and ruins. A duel and its fallout force several characters to face what they hold sacred. Bourget lets Rome itself judge them, its altars and tombs outlasting every fashion. Readers who want the full design, rather than the separate slices, take the novel here, where its pressure builds from first salon to last reckoning.
countess-kate: Countess Kate, Charlotte Yonge's novel. The countess's tale. This book preserves that story. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
court-memoirs-of-france-series-complete:
Nine sets of French court memoirs by various hands stand gathered in this Court Memoirs of France volume. Marguerite de Valois, queen of Navarre, opens the series with her own letters on the years 1565 to 1582. Pages cover the St. Bartholomew massacre, the League, and travel at a sixteenth-century court. Storytelling made her memoirs famous from their printing in 1628.

Cardinal de Retz and Madame de Montespan carry the story into the age of Louis XIV. The Duchess d'Orleans and Saint-Simon give views of that king's court. Madame du Hausset reports the courts of Louis XV and Louis XVI. Madame Campan closes the line with Marie Antoinette memoirs, written from a lady-in-waiting's post. Memoirs of the Court of St. Cloud and the Count Grammont round out the set. Readers who want history told by the people who bowed, schemed, and gossiped inside it get centuries in one file.
cumner-s-son-and-other-south-sea-folk-co:
Cumner's Son and Other South Sea Folk, complete, by Gilbert Parker, gathers his five volumes of Australian and Pacific tales in one text. Parker opens with the title story in Volume 1. Cumner is an old island official. His son inherits his influence and its enemies. Traders, chiefs, and gunboat politics fill that first long tale.

Later volumes range widely. The High Court of Budgery-Gar sits in an Australian bush camp. The Planter's Wife studies a loveless marriage under tropical heat. A Sable Spartan debates empire at a luncheon table. A Pagan of the South closes the set in New Caledonia, among convict exiles. Parker wrote these stories from his years as a journalist in Australia and the Pacific. Character, in his colonies, governs where regulations cannot reach. The whole shelf asks what an Englishman's word is worth beyond his flag.
diana-of-the-crossways-complete:
George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways, complete in forty-three chapters, portrays a witty woman fighting for her good name. Diana, an Irish beauty who keeps a famous diary, shines first at a Dublin ball. A bad marriage to Augustus Warwick leaves her separated and watched. Her friend Emma and the steady Thomas Redworth stand by her.

Diana writes books, advises the rising politician Percy Dacier, and loves him in secret. Enemies accuse her of selling a cabinet secret to the newspapers. The charge of betrayal drives the novel's crisis at the crossways of her life. Meredith closes with a final struggle for liberty and a nuptial chapter. The book defends a clever woman's honour against a gossiping world, in prose famed for its aphorisms and rapid, flashing talk.
divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-complet:
Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy stands complete in this single volume of H F Cary's translation, Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise in sequence. The contents list thirty-four cantos of Hell with Cary's notes, then thirty-three each for the other two regions. Cary, an English clergyman, published his version in the years around 1814 and changed Dante's English fortunes.

Readers travel from the dark wood through the frozen pit, up the mountain where spirits sing with mingled pleasure and pain, and into the spheres of light. Keats and Tennyson learned Dante partly from Cary. Keeping his three parts together, as here, shows the poem's architecture: sin, healing, and glory balanced across one hundred cantos.
divine-comedy-longfellow-s-translation-c:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow translated the whole Divine Comedy of Dante Alighieri, and this volume prints his Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso complete. His contents add helpful summaries: the dark forest and three beasts, Charon at Acheron, Limbo's noble castle of philosophy, and Francesca in the hurricane of the wanton. Longfellow worked in a grave, close blank verse.

The American poet labored on Dante for years, especially after his wife's death, and published the translation in 1867. His version favors fidelity over flourish, letting readers follow Dante's argument canto by canto. Notes and Italian scholarship surrounded the first edition. Generations of American students met Dante in Longfellow's lines, and the translation still reads with quiet dignity.

donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-egypt-c:
Donovan Pasha and Some People of Egypt, complete, by Gilbert Parker, gathers all four volumes of his Egyptian tales in one text. Parker explains in his introduction that the book was planned as a herald. The Weavers, his Egyptian novel, followed it in 1907. Fifteen stories stand in the contents. They run from While the Lamp Holds Out to Burn to The Light of Other Days.

Dicky Donovan moves through them all. He is the Khedive's English secretary, small and unremarkable to look at. He knows Egypt from the inside. Officers like Fielding and Wyndham succeed or blunder around him. Egyptian soldiers, sheikhs, and dancing girls get their own tales. Parker never ruled Egypt and said so. He built his Cairo from travel, reading, and soldiers' talk. The set remains his most popular short work: an occupied country rendered as a chessboard of honor, debt, and sudden violence.
dryden-s-palamon-and-arcite:
John Dryden's Palamon and Arcite, edited by George E. Eliot for school study, presents Dryden's retelling of Chaucer's Knight's Tale. Eliot, English master at the Morgan School, dedicates the volume to Henry A. Beers of Yale, who first aroused his interest in Dryden.

The preface admits the difficulty of editing a classic for schools, since colleges vary their examination demands from year to year. Eliot therefore offers a generally comprehensive outline, which teachers may fill in as they please. Students meeting Dryden for the first time will find Palamon and Arcite, the tale of two knights' rivalry in love and war, nobly told.
embers-complete:
Embers, complete, by Gilbert Parker, holds all three volumes of his collected songs and poems in one text. Parker the novelist wrote verse from the beginning of his career. The first volume opens with the title poem and Rosleen. Irish exile songs stand beside sea pieces and desert calls. Mary Callaghan and Me, Kildare, and You'll Travel Far and Wide set the early tone.

Volume 3 ends the gathering in Camden Town and at Juniper Cove. An Arab Love Song, a camel driver addressing his camel, and the Australian Stockrider widen the map. Parker's three worlds all sing here: Ireland remembered, Egypt imagined, Canada and Australia traveled. The poems are lyrics for recitation, plain in diction and strong in refrain. Read whole, Embers is the diary under the novels. The same longing for home, and the same restlessness that forbids it, drive every story Parker ever told.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-complete:
Charles Cotton's English translation gathers Michel de Montaigne's whole Essays into one large file, edited by William Carew Hazlitt. Montaigne (1533-1592), a French judge turned country landowner, built the book across twenty years of retirement. He called each short piece an essay, a trial of his judgment. His own mind serves as the main subject throughout.

All three books stand here in order, from early chapters on sorrow, idleness, and liars to late studies of vanity and experience. Friendship, cannibals, custom, cruelty, books, coaches, and repentance show the range of his curiosity. A life of Montaigne, his letters, and an editor's preface frame the essays themselves. Latin quotations crowd the pages, yet the talk stays personal and plain. Anyone who wants the complete work in one place, rather than split across separate volumes, starts with this file.
europmc-pmc7119644-REWRITE: How common is autism in American kids? The ADDM Network's 2016 watch across 11 US sites gauged autism's share among 8-year-olds nationwide. Counting cases carefully to grasp the true scope for families and schools across the country.
evan-harrington-complete:
George Meredith's Evan Harrington, complete in one volume, tells the whole story of a tailor's son in love with a lady. Melchisedec Harrington, the great Mel of Lymport, leaves his son Evan a trade, a temper, and three ambitious sisters. The eldest becomes Countess de Saldar and plots Evan's rise. Evan himself sails, travels, and shines in company.

Across forty-seven chapters Evan courts Rose Jocelyn while hiding his shop. The Jocelyns of Beckley Park stand for county pride and horror of trade. Cricket matches, picnics, letters, and duels of wit fill the middle. Evan writes himself tailor, then calls himself gentleman, as honesty slowly wins. Meredith's comedy asks whether worth lies in birth, work, or character. It remains one of his sunniest novels, dense with talk and alive with social observation.
fires-and-firemen-from-the-eclectic-maga:
The Eclectic Magazine of Foreign Literature reprinted Fires and Firemen in its May 1855 number, taking the article from the Quarterly Review. The piece reviews the annual reports of Mr. Braidwood, superintendent of London's Fire Brigade. Its stations, the article says, strike every stranger to the metropolis. A sentinel waits, and the red artillery gleams ready.

London firefighting becomes spectacle and system at once. Horses tear foaming through crowded streets, a hundred arms work the pump, and the fire-escape swings in for the shrieking figure at the window. Braidwood's reports supply the facts underneath the drama: engines, stations, and discipline. The article argues that an organized brigade, not parish engines and volunteers, saves a modern city. American readers of the Eclectic met London's model whole. It is journalism of admiration, and a founding text of professional fire service history.
frederick-chopin-as-a-man-and-musician-c:
Frederick Niecks's Frederick Chopin, as a Man and Musician, complete in the third edition of 1902, joins both volumes in one file. His first preface dates from 1888, when the work was the first full Chopin biography. A proem on Poland and the Poles precedes nineteen chapters in the first volume alone. The second volume completes the life and judges the works.

Niecks states his guiding principle plainly: facts collected, conclusions drawn, both placed before the reader. He laboured, he says, to avoid diffuseness and rhapsody, the besetting sins of writers on music. Liszt's earlier life of Chopin is weighed and found exuberant. Letters, pupils' memories, and documents carry the narrative from Warsaw to Paris and the grave. This is the scholarly Chopin, the source from which the popular ones descend. Its bulk is its virtue: everything Niecks could verify is here.
fromont-and-risler-complete:
Alphonse Daudet's Paris factory novel is presented whole in Fromont and Risler, Complete, the full English text of the Fromont Jeune et Risler Aine story. Risler the elder, a Swiss engineer of tireless honesty, joins the Fromont wallpaper firm as working partner. Georges Fromont, the heir, prefers pleasure and leaves the ledgers to others. Sidonie Chebe, the pretty girl from the shop across the street, marries Risler to reach the great house.

Inside, balls, dresses, and bills pile up while cashier Sigismond keeps the true accounts in silence. Sidonie's affair with Georges, her wedding-day waltz partner, spends the firm's money and Risler's trust together. Frantz, the younger brother who loved her first, suffers at the household's edge. Daudet follows the discovery and the honest man's end with a storyteller's speed. Readers taking the novel whole get the complete design: factory, shop, and parlor bound in one tragedy of trust.
gerfaut-complete:
Charles de Bernard won the French Academy's crown with Gerfaut, his best novel, and this complete English edition holds it whole. An essay opens the file, calling Bernard a pupil of Balzac with a lighter hand. Octave de Gerfaut, a young writer fresh from conquering Paris letters, visits the castle of Baron de Bergenheim. An attachment grows between the guest and the baron's wife.

Workman Lambernier, cursing his master by the roadside, sounds the first note of revenge. Inside the chateau, dinners and hunts cover a love that deepens by glances. The Baron's humor cracks at his own table as suspicion settles on his wife. Marillac and Mademoiselle de Corandeuil supply comedy around the tragedy. Bernard drives the design to exposure and grief. Readers taking Gerfaut whole see why the Academy prized it: Balzac's province, drawn with polish and a colder heart.
govdocs-archive_org-WOIlluminatiFreemaso:
Helen Peters wrote The Union Jack to argue that Britain's national flag is no innocent emblem. In her reading, the flag's design embodies a conspiracy that mocks Christ, and the British Empire's rulership amounted to a usurpation of Christ's rightful sovereignty.

Peters decodes the flag's crosses and colors as hidden religious statements, building her case from symbolism and scripture. The book belongs to the fringe end of writing about flags, where designs are treated as coded messages from secret powers. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers curious about that tradition of interpretation.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAWatergate_CI: Government material filed under the heading CIA Watergate makes up this file, released without a fuller description. The CIA's threads into Watergate were real: the burglars included former agency men, and Howard Hunt carried an agency past into the White House plumbers. The administration pressed the CIA to help shield the break-in investigation. Those threads filled hearing rooms for two years. The file is kept as titled, a fragment of that record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClarkWilliamKem:
Dr. William Kemp Clark directed neurosurgery at Parkland Hospital and was among the doctors who attended President Kennedy in Trauma Room One. These research notes work through his Warren Commission deposition of March 21, 1964.

The notes concentrate on his time sequences and on the press conference of November 22, 1963, where Clark announced the President's death and described the wounds as he understood them. Clark's early public words about the wounds became evidence in every later argument over the shots' direction. A researcher's notes on the deposition show the case being rebuilt from its testimony, page by page.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeathCertificat:
An FBI memorandum deals with an odd side problem after President Kennedy's death: copies of his death certificate. The Texas Registrar of Vital Statistics had been issuing copies of the certificate. Both the Secret Service and the FBI made inquiries into how those copies were being given out.

Behind the inquiries sat a suspected scheme to sell numerous copies of the document. A president's death certificate had obvious value as a souvenir or worse, and officials wanted the flow stopped or explained. The memo shows the Bureau handling the paperwork fallout of the assassination, far from the shooting itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FOIAPrivacyActR: Opening pages of Washington Hunt, a book by Bert Andrews published by Random House in New York, survive in this file. Despite the catalog label attached to it, the file does not contain the FOIA Privacy Act appeal that the label describes. What a reader gets instead is the start of Andrews's book, so the entry stands as a short excerpt under a mismatched archive label.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HollywoodReport:
Jay Carr wrote for the Hollywood Reporter on August 15, 1991 about Oliver Stone on the defensive. Stone's film JFK advanced a conspiracy account of the Kennedy assassination, and critics attacked its history before it even opened. Stone answered in the piece's headline words: I have done all my homework.

A director defending a film in the trade press is show business and history at once. Stone's JFK forced a national argument about who killed Kennedy, fought out in interviews like this one. Carr's piece preserves the defense at the height of that controversy.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-IntelligenceAge:
William Greider wrote an article headlined Again, Government Claims the Power to Snoop, with a second headline noting the FBI infiltrates an anti-draft group. His subject is the reach of government surveillance in America. An infiltrated draft-resistance group serves as his evidence that the power was being used at home.

Greider wrote for readers who remembered the exposure of domestic spying programs. Each new claim of authority, he argues, repeats an old pattern. The article preserves that argument in the press of the day, with the anti-draft infiltration as its case in point.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RedRosesFromTex:
Nerin E. Gun's book 'Red Roses From Texas' is preserved here in full text. It was published by Frederick Muller in London. Gun, a Turkish-born journalist, wrote one of the early books on the Kennedy assassination, drawing on the European view of Dallas and on his own reporting.

Early assassination books set the terms the debate still uses: doubts about the lone gunman, interest in Oswald's travels, suspicion of official haste. Gun's was among the first written from outside the United States. The full text lets readers test his account directly, rather than through later summaries. It also preserves the London edition of a book that reached American readers in the first wave of Warren Report criticism.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WATE_WATE: nsia-WATE WATE: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-philip-corso-william:
Philip J. Corso, a retired Army colonel, claimed he personally handled alien technology recovered from the Roswell crash site. Written with William J. Birnes, The Day After Roswell appeared in 1997, fifty years after the famous 1947 incident in New Mexico.

Corso says the Army quietly fed pieces of the wreckage to American industry under his direction. In his account, that seeding helped produce later tools and devices, while officials kept the source secret from the public. The book became a landmark of UFO literature and remains highly controversial, since its claims rest on Corso's word rather than documents readers can test.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Cub:
Journalist Lisa Howard built a back channel between Washington and Fidel Castro's Cuba in the early 1960s. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 624, published in April 2018. It appeared as the Castro era was ending and draws on records of her quiet work.

Howard's efforts aimed at rapprochement, a thaw between two hostile governments. The posting calls her method intimate diplomacy, meaning personal trust used where formal talks could not go. Her story shows how much Cold War diplomacy ran through private people. It also preserves the papers behind a channel that stayed hidden for years.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In 1960 an American intelligence report reached a firm conclusion about Israel's new nuclear site: it was for weapons. William Burr and Avner Cohen edited this briefing book, number 877, published in December 2024. The report dates from the site's earliest years, when its purpose was publicly denied.

Evidence here is limited to the editors, number, and the report's conclusion. That conclusion alone carries weight. It means Washington's analysts identified a weapons purpose at the start of a program Israel would not acknowledge for decades. The posting belongs to the long documentary trail of an open secret, told from inside the watching government.

How much nuclear force is enough to deter an enemy? William Burr edited this briefing book, number 779, published in October 2021, on the Navy's case for finite deterrence. Navy leaders worried that hair-trigger readiness and vulnerable missile silos could frighten an enemy into striking first.

Chief of Naval Operations Arleigh Burke argued that even the maddest Russian was deterred, because the Soviets had striven too hard to industrialize to risk devastation. A Navy report described the war plan's result as a smoking, radiating ruin at the end of two hours. The documents show admirals arguing that enough was enough, against services demanding more.

On October 6, 1977, President Jimmy Carter did something no president had done: he personally took part in a nuclear drill. The exercise, code-named Ivory Item, was a Missile Attack Conference. Carter and his top officials rehearsed the response to a simulated surprise nuclear strike on the United States.

A rehearsal at that level tests more than machinery. It forces a president to practice the gravest decision in the job, with the clock running, before any real crisis arrives. The posting preserves the record of that practice session. It shows the command system being exercised by the one person whose orders it exists to carry.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_openness: When Hungarians rose against communist rule in 1956, the United States encouraged them with broadcasts but sent no help as Soviet tanks crushed the revolt. Whether America acted wrongly, or could not have acted, is debated to this day. This briefing-book page revives that debate over American action and inaction during the revolution. The evidence here is the title alone. A companion Archive volume prints Eisenhower's private conclusion that neither military operations nor uprisings were feasible in Soviet-held Europe.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Archive_CREW: Records of a president's calls with foreign heads of state are among the most sensitive papers a White House creates, and among the first historians need. A National Security Archive briefing book page records the Archive, the watchdog group CREW, and historians jointly asking a federal judge to order those records preserved. The request belonged to the wider fight over whether the Trump White House kept the records the law requires. Only the page capture survives in this entry's evidence, marking the legal ask and its coalition.
guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-complete:
Sir Walter Scott's Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer, complete in fifty-eight chapters, opens with a young Oxford man lost in Dumfriesshire. Guy Mannering reaches Ellangowan on the night Harry Bertram is born, and casts the child's horoscope for sport. Meg Merrilies, the gypsy, takes the prophecy in earnest. The stars, she insists, will keep their appointments.

Harry is stolen by smugglers, Ellangowan falls to the lawyer Glossin's machinations, and years pass. The heir returns from India unrecognized, as Vanbeest Brown, loving Lucy Bertram, who does not know her brother. Hatteraick the smuggler, the kidnapped child's nurse, and Meg's deathbed pursuit force the truth out. Dominie Sampson, the learned, starving tutor, supplies the comedy. Scott invented the regional novel of Scotland here as much as in Waverley: dialect, law, gypsies, and coast smuggling in one design. The astrology was a joke; the prophecy was the plot.
hector-s-inheritance-or-the-boys-of-smit:
Hector's Inheritance, or the Boys of Smith Institute, by Horatio Alger Jr, opens inside Castle Roscoe, where wealth has made one man bold. Alger shows Mr Roscoe ringing for the mail and looking over his lawn and avenue of trees with exultation. All of it may be his, he tells himself, if he dares, and he owes something, he adds, to his son.

Chapter headings promise the counterweight: Hector learns a secret, resents an insult, fights a skirmish, and prepares to leave home. The inheritance of the title hangs on the scheme Roscoe is hatching in his library. Sent to the Smith Institute among its boys, Hector must hold his honesty and his claim against adult plotting. Alger writes his familiar pattern with a school setting: a wronged boy, a hidden paper trail, and fortune waiting on proof of character.
henry-clay-s-remarks-in-house-and-senate:
Henry Clay speaks twice in this short file of his remarks in Congress. The first speech, in the House on January 19, 1819, concerns the Seminole War and General Jackson's invasion of Florida. The second, in the Senate on January 16, 1837, opposes the expunging resolutions.

The expunging fight asked the Senate to black out its earlier censure of President Jackson from its own journal. Clay asks what patriotic purpose such an act could serve and warns against sanctioning violence against the record itself. His sentences show the Great Compromiser as a debater, formal, sarcastic, and constitutional. Both speeches capture Jacksonian-era battles over executive power that Clay fought for decades.
hesiod-homeric-hymns-homerica-evelyn-whi:
Translator Hugh Evelyn-White gathered Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and the Homerica in one volume. Hesiod was a Greek farmer-poet who sang of work and the gods' birth. The hymns praise single gods in epic style.

Works and Days gives farming lore mixed with myth and moral advice. The Theogony traces the gods from chaos to Zeus. The hymns honor Apollo, Hermes, and other powers. Loose fragments round out the set. The volume is a compact doorway into early Greek religion and song, older than most of the classics beside it.
history-of-greece-vol-5-grote:
George Grote, a Victorian banker turned historian, wrote a vast history of ancient Greece. Volume Five carries his story into the great age of Athens. His work reshaped how the English-speaking world saw Greek democracy.

Grote defends Athens and its leaders against older, harsher judges. He covers wars, laws, and the rise of Athenian power in detail. His prose is formal but clear and full of learning. The set remains a landmark of classical history. This volume suits readers who want the drama of Greece told by a master advocate.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1586-8:
John Lothrop Motley's chapters nine to twenty, complete in one file, carry his History of the United Netherlands through 1586 to 1589. The question whether Elizabeth should accept the sovereignty opens the sequence. Leicester's quarrels with the States, his finance, and his counsellors fill the first chapters. Paul Buys intrigues, is imprisoned, and illustrates the opposition's fate.

Drake's visit and the Babington plot lead toward the Armada year. Leicester departs, Barneveld rises, and the provinces govern themselves in his absence. Philip in his cabinet and the great fleet off Calais dominate the close. Alexander's siege of Bergen-op-Zoom ends the file in 1589. This is the dramatic heart of Motley's work, where the republic outlives its English governor and survives Spain's supreme effort. A drunken supper quarrel sits beside the fate of nations, in his manner.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1590-9:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands for 1590 to 1599, complete in chapters twenty-one to thirty-seven, covers the republic's heroic decade. The assassination of Henry III concentrates all forces as the file opens. The United Provinces struggle against Philip becomes a war for independence in earnest. Maurice reforms the army and its martial science.

Sieges at Steenwyk and Gertruydenberg show the new method at work. France's civil war, Farnese's death, and Henry IV's conversion fill the middle. Vervins, the transfer of the provinces, and Philip's death close the political arc. Van Linschoten's travels open the commercial future in the final chapter. Motley's pace quickens as his republic prospers. This is the sunniest stretch of his history, where survival turns into greatness and the Dutch become a world power.
hofmannsthal-gedichte:
Hugo von Hofmannsthal wrote poems of unearthly beauty before he was twenty, a boy genius of Viennese modernism. His Gedichte, given here in German, gather the lyrics on which that early fame rests. Transience, beauty, and the mystery of existence shimmer through the collection's brief forms.

Few poets anywhere have matched the finish of these youthful verses, written while he still signed himself Loris. Ballads, sonnets, and dreamlike lyrics move between splendor and quiet dread. The poems stand among the glories of German poetry in any century. Reading them in the original repays even modest German richly. They also explain why Vienna watched this teenager as if he were already a classic.
homo-sum-complete:
Homo Sum in complete form presents Georg Ebers and his desert novel whole, in Clara Bell's English translation. Ebers explains that work on a history of the Sinai peninsula drew him into old accounts of monks, martyrs, and hermits. One tale stayed with him: a cave dweller who accepted expulsion for a sin another man had committed, and stayed silent until the guilty man confessed.

From that seed grows Paulus, an anchorite, meaning a monk who lives alone, at the oasis of Pharan below Mount Sinai. Young Hermas, raised in the desert by his father Stephanus, strains against the narrow life and falls through Sirona, a Roman officer's wife. Paulus takes the blame and the punishment. Desert prayer, family grief, and a hard idea of love carry the full story to its close.
in-the-blue-pike-complete:
In the Blue Pike in complete form gathers the whole strolling player novel by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary T Safford. Ebers opens with Cyriax, a wandering performer punished by the Nuremberg magistrates. They cropped his tongue for blasphemy, meaning reckless speech against God. His curses now come out in sounds almost nobody can follow. His wife leads him by a chain, like a tame bear.

Lame, sick, and aging fairground folk make up the troupe. At the center stands Kuni, a rope dancer whose health and luck are failing. She nurses a sick mother and twins when their helper gives up. Then she sets out on pilgrimage, a religious journey, to Altotting and far Santiago de Compostela. The road costs her last penny. Cold nights on deck ruin her cough. Charity among the very poor carries the book.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
In the Fire of the Forge in complete form holds the whole Nuremberg romance by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers opens on the eve of St Medard's Day in 1281, with moonlight over the imperial free city. Emperor Rudolph is in residence, and the wealthy Ortlieb household sits quiet under its linden tree while soldiers are kept indoors by imperial order.

Inside that stillness, two sisters, Els and Eva Ortlieb, become the center of the tale. The knight Heinz Schorlin loves Eva, who hopes to turn him toward the Church, while slander against the sisters threatens the family honor. Servants like Biberli and Katterle carry secrets, cover stories, and errands between castle and mansion. Sieges, town hearings, and a friar telling the life of St Francis fill out a full medieval city in one volume.
inebriety-and-the-candidate:
George Crabbe's Inebriety and The Candidate collects two of his early satirical poems with an introductory address. Inebriety opens by singing the mighty spirit that stains the bloodless cheek. Winter drives every rank to its bottle: champagne for the courtier, burgundy for the colonel. Happy Colin tells ghost tales over his ale.

Crabbe follows drink through curate, shrew, and city ruler with a physician's eye — he trained as a surgeon-apothecary. The Candidate turns to a contested election, where the same bottles do political work. Crabbe addresses the reader and the Monthly Review's critics in his prefaces, touchy and ambitious. These apprentice poems already show his method: couplets as case-notes on provincial life. The realism that made The Village famous is present here in embryo, sharpened by personal knowledge of the tavern and the hustings.
jacqueline-complete:
Th. Bentzon, pen name of Marie Therese Blanc, wrote Jacqueline as a novel of girlhood and first love. This English edition holds the whole story in one file. Jacqueline de Nailles grows up in a home where her mother receives society. Family friend Hubert Marien has known her since childhood and teased her as his little wife.

Cousin Giselle de Monredon, a convent orphan, enters the household like a night moth among bright insects. Jacqueline's kindness to Giselle shows her character before love tests it further. Marien, silent and seldom pleased in society, smiles for Jacqueline as for no one else. What began as a family joke ripens into a feeling both must judge with care. Bentzon keeps the drama in drawing rooms and duties rather than grand events. Readers prized her for tender studies of young women, and Jacqueline stands as her signature work.
john-caldigate:
John Caldigate is a novel by Anthony Trollope, mapped in forty-two chapters. It begins at Folking and Puritan Grange, with Daniel Caldigate and the Shands. A chapter called The Goldfinder points the hero toward the goldfields. Mrs. Smith, the Three Attempts, and Reaching Melbourne follow in quick order.

The middle chapters move between Australia and home: Polyeuka Hall, Ahalala, and Mademoiselle Cettini. Then Caldigate comes back to weddings, a new heir, and news from the gold mines. Later titles darken into prison, an escape, restitution, and a trial. The last chapters are named for the trial's first and second days. Trollope stakes the whole plot on whether Caldigate's past will destroy his marriage.
john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-complete:
John Lothrop Motley, A Memoir is Oliver Wendell Holmes's life of the American historian, in a complete edition. Holmes based it on a sketch written for the Massachusetts Historical Society. He warns readers that this version treats controversies the Society could not enter. It also adds many details beyond a tribute's usual limits, while remaining an outline.

The first chapter covers Motley's birth and early years, from 1814 to 1827. Holmes starts with the family line: John Motley came from Belfast to Falmouth, now Portland, Maine. Two grandsons moved to Boston in 1802 and traded in partnership for nearly fifty years. Holmes even tells how a quick-witted maid saved the family line during the 1708 attack on Haverhill.
joshua-complete:
Joshua is a historical novel by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford. Ebers tells in his preface how the book grew from his own travels. Following the traces of the departing Hebrews in the desert, he conceived a romance of their wanderings. He first sketched the idea, he says, on the back of a camel.

The novel treats the Exodus story in fictional form, with Joshua at its center. Ebers meant the book for his friend Gustav Baur, a professor disabled by illness. Baur died before it was finished, so the preface offers it to his memory instead. Their talks about the story of the Exodus, Ebers writes, numbered among his good hours.
kalevala-the-epic-poem-of-finland-comple:
The Kalevala is the epic poem of Finland, translated into English by John Martin Crawford in 1888. Elias Lönnrot, named as the work's maker, gathered Finland's old sung tales into one epic. This complete edition runs to fifty runes, or songs. The proem and Rune One open with the birth of Wainamoinen, the old singer-hero.

The contents move through Wainamoinen's sowing, his contest with Youkahainen, and the fate of Aino. Ilmarinen the smith forges the Sampo, a wonder-working mill, in Rune Ten. Lemminkainen's wooing, death, and restoration fill a long middle stretch. Wedding songs, the brewing of beer, and the making of the harp follow. Crawford's verse carries Finland's national epic to English readers whole.
kenelm-chillingly-complete:
Kenelm Chillingly is Edward Bulwer Lytton's novel of a young man's search for a way to live, here complete in one volume. It opens with his father, Sir Peter Chillingly of Exmundham, a baronet and fellow of learned societies. Sir Peter married Caroline Brotherton young, against his own wish, at his parents' request. Her fortune doubled his income and bought two farms.

Caroline, the book says, was accomplished: piano, water-colours, French and Italian, all performed with taste. Lonely after his wife's death, Sir Peter turned to study for company. Kenelm grows up their only child, odd, bookish, and restless. The novel follows him out of Exmundham to test the world's wisdom against his own strange questions.
knickerbocker-s-history-of-new-york-comp:
Washington Irving published Knickerbocker's History of New York in December 1809. He was twenty-six, and the book first won him wide credit. It pretends to be the work of Diedrich Knickerbocker, a Dutch historian.

Irving tells New York's Dutch past as comic history, with satire hidden inside. Walter Scott praised its humor and compared it with Dean Swift. He read it aloud to guests until their sides ached with laughing. The book still shows Irving's gift for mixing jokes, local pride, and sly criticism. The mock-serious tone lets Irving praise and tease New York at once. Later American humor owes much to this early success.
l-abbe-constantin-complete:
Ludovic Halévy wrote The Abbé Constantin, a French novel read here in English. This complete edition opens with a preface by E. Legouvé of the French Academy. A long sketch of Halévy's life follows.

Halévy was born in Paris in 1834, into a famous artistic family. He left government work to write for the stage, then turned to fiction. His long partnership with Henri Meilhac produced many plays and operas. This novel shows his later fiction side, warm and humane in tone. The preface and life sketch frame the novel as a prized French work. English readers met Halévy here as both dramatist and novelist.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's complete Leila appeared in 1838. Its five books tell one tale of the siege of Granada. Contents run from an enchanter and warrior to the final battle.

Book One sets lovers, a king, and a father against ambition. Book Two brings ambush, strife, and capture in the Christian camp. Later books test Leila before priests, queens, and armies. Her Jewish faith and her love cross the war's lines. This single file holds the whole romance in order. David Widger produced this complete Gutenberg text. Five books in one file suit readers who dislike split volumes.
literature-and-life-complete:
William Dean Howells collects a lifetime of essays in this complete volume. Man of Letters in Business opens the contents. Confessions of a Summer Colonist and The Young Contributor follow. Anomalies of the Short Story examines his own craft.

Travel pieces recall Dutch hotels and Spanish prisoners of war. American literary centers and standard household effects get essays. Short stories and sketches mix with criticism and fiction studies. Howells doubts readers will feel the inner solidarity he senses. Puritanism in American fiction and plagiarism's psychology appear late. Storage and river songs on the Ohio close the miscellany.
lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-complete:
George Meredith's novel Lord Ormont and His Aminta tells of a proud old soldier and the young wife who refuses to stay in his shadow. Aminta first meets Lord Ormont as a schoolgirl who worships him as a hero. She later marries him, but he treats the marriage as something to hide. The young secretary Matthew Weyburn, once her school tutor, loves her still.

Across five books the story moves through drawing rooms, country houses, and roads around Steignton. Lady Charlotte, Ormont's sharp-tongued sister, watches the struggle and stirs it. Aminta slowly claims the place of a wife, not a secret. Meredith packs the tale with wit, talk, and sharp views of pride. It shows a marriage tested by one man's pride and one woman's spirit.
lucretia-complete:
Lucretia, or The Children of Night, is a novel by Edward Bulwer Lytton. This complete text carries his preface to the 1853 edition. Lytton says he began it beside The Caxtons, as a pendant piece. Both books study how early training shapes a life.

The Caxtons shows the sunny side of home influence. Lucretia shows the dark side, through awe and distress. Its people are children of night, marked by bad example. Lytton complains that readers missed his moral design at first. The novel is a tragedy of character formed in childhood. It stands as the shadow twin of his cheeriest family tale.
madame-chrysantheme-complete:
Madame Chrysanthème, complete in this edition, carries a preface by Albert Sorel. Sorel was a member of the French Academy. A sketch here tells how Pierre Loti was really Louis-Marie-Julien Viaud. Born at Rochefort in 1850, he served in the French Navy until 1900.

Shy as a young midshipman, he was nicknamed for a small Indian flower. The novel itself is his diary of one Japanese summer. In Nagasaki he took a temporary wife, called Chrysanthème. Loti writes as an impressionist, in dainty and melancholy prose. His Japan is beautiful, strange, and never quite possessed. The book made him famous across Europe and America.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-com:
Margery, called Gred, is a tale of old Nuremberg by Georg Ebers. Clara Bell translated it from the German for English readers. Ebers frames the tale with a Venetian antiquary's manuscript sheets. The translator strove to avoid words too modern for the fifteenth century.

Margery Schopper tells her own life in the free imperial city. Her brother Herdegen, her cousin Maud, and her friend Ann share it. Love, family pride, and city custom shape her fortunes. Emperors enter Nuremberg, and maidens greet them with flowers. Ebers rebuilt old Germany from deep historical study. The complete tale is a rich portrait of a girl and her city.
marine-protozoa-from-woods-hole-bulletin:
Marine Protozoa from Woods Hole is a scientific paper by Gary N. Calkins. It appeared in the Bulletin of the United States Fish Commission in 1901. Calkins taught zoology at Columbia University. The work came from the Fish Commission's laboratory at Woods Hole, Massachusetts.

Little, he says, had been done in America on marine protozoa. A few observers — Kellicott, Stokes, and Peck — had worked before him. Peck had shown how these tiny creatures feed larger sea life. Calkins catalogues the one-celled animals of Woods Hole waters. Species are described and pictured for other workers. The paper is a careful foundation stone of American protozoology.
marjorie-at-seacote:
Marjorie at Seacote is a girls' book by Carolyn Wells, copyrighted in 1912. Grosset and Dunlap issued it among her Marjorie series. Wells also wrote the famous Patty books for older girls. A frontispiece shows a boy called King bowing low, cape falling.

' Most liege majesty,' he begins, in the children's shore-side play. Seacote is the Maynard family's summer place by the sea. Marjorie's vacation brings games, guests, scrapes, and small triumphs. Wells writes with the light touch her readers loved. Each chapter is a bright bead on a summer string. The Marjorie books were staples of American girlhood reading. This one smells of salt air and holiday freedom.
mark-twain-a-biography-complete:
Mark Twain: A Biography, complete in this text, is Albert Bigelow Paine's authorized life. Its subtitle promises the personal and literary life of Samuel Langhorne Clemens. Paine dedicated it to Clara Clemens, Twain's daughter. She upheld his purpose to write history rather than eulogy.

An acknowledgment thanks Howells, Twichell, Goodman, and other old friends. Six years and more went into the making of these volumes. Paine lived in Twain's house and heard his memories at first hand. The life runs from Hannibal boyhood to the Stormfield farewell. Letters, anecdotes, and sorrows fill its thousands of pages. It remains the foundation of all Twain biography.
marse-henry-an-autobiography-complete:
Henry Watterson, the Kentucky editor known as Marse Henry, tells his whole life story here. The complete book was signed from Mansfield in 1919. It starts with his birth and his first years in Washington.

Early chapters recall John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson, and James K. Polk. Later ones move through slavery, the fall of the Whig party, and Lincoln taking office. Watterson writes as a man who knew the actors and watched the old capital change. His post in Congress and his years in Paris come later in the tale. Few American editors of his day left so full a record of their times.
master-of-his-fate:
J. Maclaren Cobban published Master of His Fate in 1890. He wrote the book in London in November 1889. A warm note gives the tale's good doctor a real model.

Cobban says the doctor is drawn from his friend Z. Mennell. He calls him a born surgeon, alert, kind, and quick to forgive. The plot starts at the Hyacinth Club with Julius Courtney. A strange case, a man in a crowd, and Lady Mary Fane follow. Strange scenes in Curzon Street and a confession close the heads. Cobban blends a love thread with cases that test the doctor's art.
memoirs-correspondence-and-manuscripts-o:
General Lafayette's family published his Memoirs, Correspondence and Manuscripts. George Washington Lafayette signed the family's short note at the front. Rights for the American edition were entered in 1837 by William A. Duer.

The family says they kept the papers whole, with no notes added. They call the act a solemn homage to his memory. The American edition adds letters left out of the Paris and London sets. Those letters treat the American Revolution and add worth for readers here. Some added letters had not been seen in print before this set. Liberty's friends are the readers the family had in mind.
memoirs-of-aaron-burr-complete:
Matthew L. Davis wrote the Memoirs of Aaron Burr, in two volumes. Rights were entered in 1836 in the Southern District of New York. A front picture shows Burr, and an epigraph from Shakespeare heads it.

Davis knew Burr well for forty years, by his own account. Burr asked him to note down his political life after 1812. Jefferson's Ana roused Burr over the House contest of 1801. Burr gave Davis his private papers and offered to dictate parts of his tale. Davis soon saw Burr cared most for his soldier's name. That pride shapes what the two volumes choose to stress.
memoirs-of-general-william-t-sherman-com:
William T. Sherman wrote his memoirs and signed them at St. Louis. The preface is dated January 21, 1875, ten years after the war. He gave the book to his comrades, volunteers and regulars alike.

Sherman says no good full history of the war can yet be had. The War Department holds the records, and they come out slowly, he notes. His book gives his own memories, checked against his private notes. A second edition preface says he revised it ten years on, in light of critique. He asks trust from survivors of the cause on both sides. Fairness to foe as well as friend is his stated aim.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Madame de Montespan's memoirs appear here in a complete English set. She calls them the historic memoirs of the court of Louis XIV. A list of pictures names Moliere, Racine, and Bossuet among the faces.

The translator's preface asks for a fairer view of her than most give. Her random notes, he says, show no care for strict time order. Yet they draw a self portrait of the lady whose beauty held a king. Her sharp tongue, he adds, made duchesses quail at court. Charles II and Madame de Maintenon stand in the picture list too. The set aims at the whole court, not its lady alone.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-complete: Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne, Napoleon's private secretary, wrote the Memoirs of Napoleon Bonaparte. R. W. Phipps edited the complete set, dated 1891 in the sample. The hosted sample preserves the contents list only. It names the 1836 and 1885 prefaces and a first volume spanning 1769 to 1800. No readable memoir text appears in the sample held here. This note stays with those front page facts for that reason.
memorials-and-other-papers-complete:
Thomas De Quincey's Memorials and Other Papers appears here in a complete set. A letter from the author to his American editor opens volume one. He gives his papers to that house for America alone.

He thanks them for gathering his scattered works into one set. That task, he says, his own nerves had made hopeless for him. He also thanks them for a share of the profits, freely given. Contents hold The Orphan Heiress, Oxford, The Pagan Oracles, and Greece. A visit to the Priory stands inside The Orphan Heiress heads. Scattered magazine work finds a home in this one set.
michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-swords-com:
Gilbert Parker's romance grew from a brief record at the Walloon Church in Southampton. The record told of Huguenots who fled France and found refuge in England. Parker wove around Michel de la Foret and Angele Aubert what he calls a bright cloud of romance. The tale is set in the days of Queen Elizabeth.

Parker first published the story in Harper's Weekly, then doubled its length for book form. The enlarged volume took the title A Ladder of Swords. He wrote the original in seclusion on the island of Jersey. This complete edition joins the shorter tale and its expansion into one romantic history.
mingo-and-other-sketches-in-black-and-wh:
Joel Chandler Harris, famous as Uncle Remus, published these sketches in an author's edition at Edinburgh in 1899. The title story, Mingo, is a sketch of life in middle Georgia. Three more pieces follow: At Teague Poteet's, A Piece of Land, and Blue Dave. The settings run from Georgia farms to the Hog Mountain range.

Mingo opens with the narrator revisiting Crooked Creek Church in 1876. He finds the congregation aged by the years of desolation after the Civil War. Girls of 1860 have become careworn matrons. Harris writes about Black and white Southerners together, in the local-color manner that made his reputation.
monsieur-de-camors-complete:
Octave Feuillet's society novel appears here complete, with a preface by Maxime Du Camp of the French Academy. The preface calls Feuillet the leader of the idealistic school in the nineteenth century. It praises his observation, knowledge of humanity, and incomparable charm. His style is judged neat, pure, brilliant, and concise at once.

Feuillet was born at Saint-Lô in 1821 and first wrote dramas with Dumas's circle. He became an unmatched analyst of feminine character, the preface says. Monsieur de Camors, his famous novel, follows a brilliant, cynical aristocrat through Parisian society. The complete text joins the three separately issued volumes in one.
monsieur-madame-and-be-be-complete:
Gustave Droz's sketches of courtship and marriage appear here complete, with a biographical preface by Camille Doucet. Droz was born in Paris in 1832, son of a celebrated sculptor. He trained as a painter before abandoning art for authorship. His sketches in La Vie Parisienne made him famous as an exquisite storyteller of family life.

The sketches, gathered as Monsieur, Madame, et Bébé in 1866, were crowned by the French Academy. They passed through many editions. Book One opens with the narrator's first supper party. Droz analyzes bachelor and married life with vivacity and sparkle, and the complete volume follows the young couple into parenthood.
mr-crewe-s-career-complete:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, wrote this political novel of reform in a fictional New England state. The complete text opens with the Honourable Hilary Vane of Ripton. Vane, a widowed lawyer of sixty-five, has never held office yet holds immense quiet power. His housekeeper Euphrasia Cotton rules the long white house they share at opposite ends.

Against Vane's old order rises Humphrey Crewe, a wealthy young reformer. Crewe attacks the Northeastern Railroads' grip on the state's politics. Churchill follows hearings, campaigns, and a governor's race across three books. The novel dramatizes the Progressive Era fight between railroad money and popular government, in one full volume.
mr-trunnell-mate-of-the-ship-pirate:
T. Jenkins Hains wrote this sea tale, issued in 1900. The narrator is a young mate stuck on shore in Melbourne. He has sailed seven years but never tasted rum. All he owns is a pea coat, a pipe, and an old quadrant.

Work is scarce, and mates are many in port. He walks the wharves past fine clipper ships, hunting a berth. At last he signs with the ship Pirate and its mate Trunnell. Hains had written other sea books like The Wind-jammers. The tale promises hard ships, rough crews, and life told by a working sailor.
mrs-falchion-complete:
Gilbert Parker wrote this, his first novel, in 1892 and 1893. His introduction recalls the age of the three-volume novel. Libraries bought more copies than the public did then. Parker refused serial printing so the book could be judged whole.

Critics took note at once, and one paper called him a coming novelist. The Athenaeum praised its study of character. Parker kept that praise dear for years. The tale itself centers on the Mrs. Falchion of the title. This complete text joins both parts in one file, with Parker's own account of how the book was born.
my-novel-complete:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton opens this vast novel inside Uncle Roland's tower hall. Mr. Caxton turns a great globe for his own recreation. Pisistratus, the young narrator, watches his family at night. His mother holds up a small frock she has trimmed.

Blanche leans on her mother but eyes Pisistratus instead. Uncle Roland is deep in some third volume of a novel. Mr. Squills studies the money market in the Times. The first chapter shows how the novel came to be written. From this warm family stage, Lytton unrolls a long tale of English life, love, and ambition across many books.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-comple:
Charles M. Skinner gathers all his American folklore volumes in this complete set. The contents start along the Hudson and its hills. Rip Van Winkle, Catskill gnomes, and a witch lead off. Ghost ships, headless riders, and storm tales crowd the list.

Later parts cross the whole young nation, region by region. Treasure, Puritan lands, the South, and the Pacific slope all appear. Skinner took tales from papers, histories, and local tellers. He polished each into a storyteller's short piece. V1 calls it the fullest single gathering of its kind. For lovers of American legend, it is a deep, well-stocked storybook.
myths-and-myth-makers-old-tales-and-supe:
John Fiske explains old tales through the new science of myth study. He dedicates the book to William Dean Howells, his dear friend. They had spent autumn evenings among werewolves and trolls, he recalls. The preface calls the papers rambling and unsystematic by design.

Fiske says he cut hard debates short to spare the reader. Philology's thorns would block the crooked lanes of inquiry, he jokes. Werewolves, fairies, and folk beliefs get traced to nature and speech. V1 dates the study to 1872 and praises its clarity and charm. It was a pioneering work of popular science writing.
napoleon-bonaparte:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this life of Napoleon Bonaparte for common readers. Abbott was a popular American historian of plain style. His book traces the Corsican artillery officer's whole arc. V1 sums it as a rise from Corsica to St. Helena.

Napoleon became master of Europe by genius and ambition. Then overreach, war, and defeat brought him to exile. Abbott tells the tale with moral force and clear order. Battles, codes, and courts fill the middle chapters. The life ends in ruin on a lone Atlantic rock. It is a clear, brisk life of a world-shaking man, long used in schools.
nasa-tm-19650020046-vacuum-compatibility:
Staff in Marshall's Propulsion and Vehicle Engineering Laboratory issued this second study, dated June 24, 1965, on how solid materials behave in vacuum. Many solids slowly give off gas and lose weight in vacuum, a process that can foul instruments or weaken a part. Sixty-two solid materials were tested for the rate and extent of that loss.

A designer needs to know which materials stay stable in space conditions. Weight loss in vacuum is a direct, practical measure. Results for many materials in one report allow fair comparison. Such screening data quietly shape material choices for spacecraft, long before any flight hardware is built.
nasa-tm-19650024321-electron-microprobe-:
Richard A Schmitt, of the Space Sciences Division at Ames, presented this paper in Moscow in July 1965. His laboratory studied micrometeorites and cosmic dust with an electron microprobe. The probe can name the elements inside a grain far too small to see. Samples were fine particles thought to come from beyond Earth.

Schmitt places the work inside a broad program on the chemistry of extraterrestrial matter. What dust is made of hints at how the solar system formed. His paper was given at an international chemistry congress. It shows American space science being reported abroad, in person, at the height of the space race.
nasa-tm-19660012350-naca-conference-on-a:
Papers from a NACA conference at the Langley Aeronautical Laboratory are compiled in this volume, declassified under a stamp dated April 6, 1966. NACA was NASA's forerunner in aircraft research. The conference covered aircraft loads, flutter, and structures. Floyd L Thompson chaired one session, and Richard V Rhode is named among the paper authors in the contents.

Loads tell engineers how hard air pushes on a structure. Flutter is a dangerous shaking that can tear a wing apart. Papers on all three topics were presented and then gathered here. Compilations like this one spread conference results to engineers who could not attend, across the aircraft industry.
nasa-tm-19670022514-performance-of-three:
Bernhard H. Anderson and David N. Bowditch report wind-tunnel experiments on supersonic air inlets in this memorandum. The inlets are round, axisymmetric designs that compress air entirely inside the duct. All three were designed for Mach 2.5 and differed only in the length of the supersonic diffuser.

The study sought the best bleed system, easier starting, and good control signals. The best bleed paired a ram scoop on the cowl with a flush bleed on the centerbody, set opposite each other past the throat. The middle-length inlet gave the best pressure recovery. Starting demanded heavy cowl bleed, because strong compressions separated the flow.
nasa-tm-19680000890-the-response-of-the-:
S. Chandra and B. V. Krishnamurthy, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in August 1967. It asks how the upper atmosphere's temperature responds when solar output and geomagnetic activity change. Temperatures were derived from satellite drag, since the thin air slows satellites by amounts that reveal its density and warmth.

Ground-based radio fluxes stood in as indices of solar extreme ultraviolet radiation. One period was also checked directly against OSO 1 satellite measurements. A planetary magnetic index measured geomagnetic activity. Splitting the data into long and short term parts gave a clean answer. Long term temperature swings tracked the radio flux strongly, peaking at one radio frequency. Short term swings, by contrast, tracked magnetic activity closely and ignored the radio flux. The study thus separates slow solar heating from fast magnetic disturbance.
nasa-tm-19680011748-interaction-effects-:
D. R. Englund, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a Cleveland electronics conference in April 1968. Numbered TM X-52428, it treats interaction effects in measurement systems: the way hooking up an instrument disturbs the very thing being measured. Englund frames the topic as the problem of matching an instrument to a system so the disturbance stays minimal.

Every sensor draws some power or energy from its system, so no measurement leaves its system fully untouched. The disturbance can change the value being measured, as when a plain voltmeter drags a voltage down. Or it can change the system's behavior itself, as when test gear stops an oscillator. Englund's discussion centers on the first kind, described through the concept of loading, set by properties such as impedance or stiffness. Practical examples span measurements of electrical amounts, temperature, force, pressure, and flow rate.
nasa-tm-19680025095-filter-properties-of:
Bodo Kruger wrote this January 1968 preprint, numbered X-561-68-141, on the filter properties of least squares fitted polynomials. Fitting a smooth curve to noisy data by least squares is a daily tool in tracking work. Kruger asks exactly how that smoothing acts as a filter, passing some parts of a signal while removing others.

As a high pass filter, the fit can strip out a spacecraft's orbit and leave pure tracking noise for study. Kruger gives equations for the curve freedom needed, and tests the leftover error on a lunar orbit. As a low pass filter, the fit compresses noisy data into fewer points. He shows the usual midpoint choice is not the least biased one.
nasa-tm-19680065332-tiros-the-first-weat:
TIROS, the first weather satellite, is introduced in this NASA booklet. TIROS stands for Television Infrared Observation Satellite. Its spacecraft use television cameras to watch Earth's cloud cover and sensors to measure infrared radiant energy. TIROS I launched on April 1, 1960, opening a new era in weather observation.

The satellite weighed nearly three hundred pounds and flew about four hundred miles up. It looked like a bass drum with needle-like antennas on its sides. Two independent camera systems photographed cloud cover over huge areas. Pictures were sent to ground stations or stored on a small tape recorder for later readout. The U.S. Weather Bureau used the photographs for forecasting work.
nasa-tm-19690017653-the-tems-apollo-satu:
Bobby Junkin, of the Computation Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, reports tracking system error model results in this March 1969 memorandum, TM X-53818. The TEMS method uses multiple regression analysis on Apollo-Saturn IB flight tests. Ground trackers follow each launch, but their readings carry errors that engineers must measure before the flight data can be trusted.

The report is the fifth in a continuing series, carrying the results through the AS-205 flight. Junkin first establishes the tracker errors from the flight data themselves. He then fits functional expressions that describe those errors as compact models. Guidelines for trimming the models, he reports, produced generally acceptable results. An appendix gives the full AS-205 test outcome.
nasa-tm-19690026064-recent-improvements-:
Rodger A. Cliff of Goddard Space Flight Center reports recent improvements in the SDP-3 computer in this August 1969 preprint, X-711-69-320. The SDP-3 is a small serial computer built for unmanned science spacecraft. It was to fly as an engineering experiment on the IMP-I spacecraft, handling data acquisition for four science experiments aboard.

Six instruction changes improved operation with little added hardware, Cliff reports. They include fuller indirect addressing, byte-wise steps, and better index handling. New shift parts saved hardware and power, though left-shifting steps were dropped. A special times-table step let one register be dropped for good. Altogether the changes cut power use and removed hundreds of circuits, he states.
nasa-tm-19700018116-outgassing-studies-o:
Goddard Space Flight Center staff issued this preprint in February 1970 on outgassing from polymer systems picked for Goddard spacecraft. Outgassing is the slow release of trapped gas and vapor from a material in vacuum. Released matter can settle on optics and other gear, so builders screen materials before flight.

The tests heated materials in vacuum for a full day and caught what condensed on a cool surface. Many glass-filled plastics, the report finds, gave off very little gas. Two room-temperature curing silicone potting compounds also scored low, while many rubbery silicones passed only after a hot post-cure. Methacrylates proved acceptable as optical elements, and other working systems are covered too.
nasa-tm-19710011472-shock-vibration-and-:
A J Stromquist of the Lewis Research Center and C L Foss of Aerojet General Corporation reported these load tests in March 1971. Their subject was the lubricant and coolant pump of the SNAP-8 space power system. SNAP-8 was a nuclear electric power plant meant for space missions. The pump had to survive launch and still work.

The team shook, shocked, and spun the pump under the SNAP-8 test rules. Performance checks ran before and after the full test series. The pump showed no clear change in performance. Staff then took it apart and inspected it closely. They found no physical damage that would limit its working life.
nasa-tm-19710025557-small-applications-t:
Small Applications Technology Satellite, or SATS, is an interim study report from the Goddard Space Flight Center, dated May 1970. A Goddard team carried out the study, with working groups for communications, navigation, geodesy, meteorology, and earth resources. The program aimed to develop new sensors, experiments, and spacecraft technology on a small satellite.

Promising ideas would prove themselves through orbital flight tests before larger missions depended on them. That approach lets engineers check hardware in real space conditions at modest cost. The study drew on informal contacts across industry and other NASA centers, from Lockheed and Hughes to Langley and Lewis. Each working group weighed how a small satellite could serve its own application area.
nasa-tm-19720006898-oxidation-vaporizati:
Fred J Kohl and Carl A Stearns of the Lewis Research Center studied how protective coatings waste away in December 1971, as NASA TM X-67980. Their samples were columbium alloys coated with a silicide layer. Such coatings guard hot parts against oxygen attack. At extreme heat the coating itself slowly vaporizes. The team heated samples and caught the vapors for analysis.

At very low oxygen pressure, the main vapor was gaseous silicon monoxide. At higher pressures, the collected deposits held chromium, silicon, iron, and tungsten species. The authors also built equilibrium diagrams for each metal involved. Their calculations matched the experiments in general. Above a set pressure, chromium species caused most of the weight loss.
nasa-tm-19720017774-space-applications-i:
R A Minzner and J D Oberholtzer of the Electronics Research Center in Cambridge compiled this handbook, issued in May 1972 as NASA TM X-2066. It gathers short profiles of instrument systems and experiments for space use. Designers planning a mission needed to know what instruments already existed. Reinventing proven hardware wastes money and time. This compendium answered that need in one volume. Its entries came in a single standard format.

One hundred fifty eight systems and experiments are profiled. Each profile holds entries for twenty six administrative items. It also holds thirty nine science or engineering items. That shared structure lets readers compare unlike instruments quickly. The profiles are organized for ready reference. Mission planners across NASA could search it before funding new designs.
night-and-morning-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton wrote Night and Morning, and this copy holds the complete novel in one file. Its contents open with a preface to the edition of 1845. The story then runs in books, each split into numbered chapters. Book one starts with an introductory chapter.

The title sets night against morning as the tale's frame. Lytton's novels of his era mixed high life, crime, and strong feeling in long, careful prose. A five book span, as the contents show, gave him room for a wide cast. Readers who want the whole work at once, rather than in parts, are served by this complete copy.
night-watches-complete:
W. W. Jacobs published Night Watches in 1911, a set of tales named here in full. Back to Back opens the contents, then Keeping Watch and The Understudy. The Weaker Vessel, Stepping Backwards, and The Three Sisters follow. The Unknown, The Vigil, Easy Money, and His Other Self close the list.

Picture captions give the flavour in dialect: a wife gasps at a deed done by daylight. A man hopes two women will not meet, poor thing. The first tale hides Mrs Scutts behind a curtain, watching a cab with uneasy wonder. Jacobs writes of sailors, night watchmen, and small cheats, in a comic voice readers loved.
no-defense-complete:
Gilbert Parker wrote No Defense as a novel in three books, and this copy holds it complete. Book one opens with two men meeting, then a messenger's coming. A quarrel and a duel follow, then the killing of Erris Boyne. Dyck, the hero, lands in prison, and a letter comes from Sheila.

Book two sends Dyck Calhoun into the world again, toward the West Indies. An hour before a mutiny and an admiral's say crowd that book. Book three moves to Salem, where Lord Mallow steps in and a clash of race comes. Sheila and Noreen each have their say. A talk with the governor nears the close.
normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its-anci:
Gordon Home depicted Normandy in words and pictures, dating his work at Epsom in October 1905. This copy holds the complete book, The Scenery and Romance of Its Ancient Towns. Lists of coloured and line illustrations come before the chapters. Chapter one takes up some features of Normandy as a whole.

By the banks of the Seine comes next, then Rouen, the ancient capital. Evreux, Lisieux, and romantic Falaise follow in turn. The road runs from Argentan to Avranches, then to Mont St Michel. Coutances, St Lo, Bayeux, and Caen fill later chapters. Notes on the history of Normandy close the book. Home mixes road notes with old tales of each town.
northern-lights-complete:
Gilbert Parker's Northern Lights gathers tales in five volumes, and this copy holds them all. Volume one opens with A Lodge in the Wilderness and Once at Red Man's River. Later volumes hold Qu'Appelle, George's Wife, and Marcile. A Man, a Famine, and a Heathen Boy stands in volume four.

Parker's introduction says the book belongs a generation after Pierre and His People. The old isolated life of Pierre's day ended, he writes, when the railway came. Towns, cities, and a flood of settlers changed the Far West. On a 1905 visit he saw even the railway era's marks fading. He wrote these tales to catch that fleeting old life.
odd-craft-complete:
William Wymark Jacobs gathered fourteen comic tales in Odd Craft. The complete book appeared with pictures by Will Owen. The contents list stories such as The Money-Box and The Castaway. Other titles include Lawyer Quince and Breaking a Spell. Most tales draw on sailors, villages, and small schemes.

Jacobs writes in a dry, funny voice with sharp dialogue. Sailors try to save money and mostly fail. Lawyers, lovers, and rivals fall into neat traps. Each short tale turns on a trick or mistake. The book is a full sample of his popular humor. Owen's pictures add to the humor of the printed edition.
old-mortality-complete:
